verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that subḥān is the verbal noun of tasbīḥ: declaring God free from everything unworthy of His holiness. Though it can be used as an exclamation, here it is glorification, because glorification governs the passage. Isrāʾ and sary mean travel by night; laylan indicates that the journey, including its return, occurred within one night before dawn. The Farthest Mosque is Jerusalem, whose precincts are blessed, and it is called “farthest” because it was the most distant mosque from the Sacred Mosque for the Prophet and his original audience in Mecca.

The journey’s purpose was to show the Prophet some—not all—of God’s signs; the context and the related statement, Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord (53:18), indicate their greatness. God is “the Hearing, the Seeing” because He heard His servant’s supplication and saw the inner state that merited this distinctive honor. The shift from the third person to the first-person plural in “of which We have blessed the precincts, so that We may show to him” signals that the journey and the showing of the signs issued from the court of divine grandeur, might, and authority: God manifested Himself to the Prophet through His greatest signs. The verse thus commands thorough glorification of the One who took His servant Muḥammad in a single night from the Sacred Mosque to Jerusalem, to show him the greatest signs by His power, because He knew him worthy of this honor.

Imam al-Ṣādiq is reported to have narrated a long account of the journey. Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel brought the burāq, which Gabriel rebuked when it startled, saying that no prophet like Muḥammad had ridden or would ride it. Accompanied by Gabriel, the Prophet was shown signs of heaven and earth. He ignored a caller on his right, a caller on his left, and a woman adorned with all worldly finery; he also heard a terrifying sound. Gabriel had him pray at Mount Sinai, where God spoke to Moses, and at Bethlehem, where Jesus son of Mary was born. At Jerusalem he tied the burāq where prophets tied their mounts, found Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and other prophets, and was placed forward by Gabriel to lead them in prayer.

In this report, the Prophet chose milk rather than water or wine from three cups; Gabriel interpreted this as guidance for him and his community. The caller on the right represented Jewish proselytization, the caller on the left Christian proselytization, and the adorned woman the world (dunyā); had he turned to any of them, his community would have followed that path. The frightening noise was a rock cast into hell seventy years earlier which had then reached its bottom. It is said that the Messenger of God did not laugh thereafter until his death.

The narration continues that the Prophet ascended through the heavens. In the lowest heaven he met Ismāʿīl, its guardian, then Mālik, the custodian of hell, who had never smiled since being assigned to it. At the Prophet’s request, Mālik displayed hell, from which a flame surged upward until the Prophet asked that it be covered again. He met Adam, who was shown his descendants; he also met the angel of death, who said that God had subjected the entire universe to him as a dirham is subject to its holder, and that he visits every house repeatedly until none of its people remains. Gabriel told the Prophet that what follows death is more overwhelming than death itself.

The Prophet was shown people receiving consequences corresponding to their deeds: those who chose unlawful food over lawful food; slanderers and backbiters whose flesh was cut and fed to them; people who slept without the Evening Prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿishāʾ), smashing their heads with rocks; those who unjustly consumed orphans’ property, fed with fire; usurers, unable to rise because of their swollen bellies and exposed to fire morning and evening; and women suspended by their breasts for introducing into their husbands’ lineages children who were not their husbands’. He saw angels wholly occupied in praise and glorification, humbled before God. He also saw an angel half fire and half ice, neither destroying the other, who prayed that God unite the hearts of believing servants; two angels prayed respectively for compensation for the charitable and loss for those who withhold charity.

The report places John and Jesus in the second heaven, Joseph in the third, Enoch in the fourth, Aaron in the fifth, Moses in the sixth, and Abraham in the seventh beside al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr. All welcomed the Prophet and prayed for him. The Prophet saw vast seas of light, darkness, and thunderous snow; Gabriel told him that what he saw was only one creation among God’s creations, that what remained unseen was greater, and that veils stood between God and creation. He also saw a vast angel in the form of a rooster, whose praise at dawn was echoed by earthly roosters.

At al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr the Prophet prayed two rakʿahs. Some of his companions wore new garments and entered, while others wore ragged garments and remained outside. He then encountered the rivers al-Kawthar and al-Raḥmah, drank from one and washed from the other, and entered the Garden. He saw the houses of himself and his household, a servant-girl belonging to Zayd b. Ḥārithah, immense birds and fruits, and the Ṭūbā Tree, whose branches reach every house in the Garden. Gabriel described its awe-inspiring seas as veils through which God veils Himself; without them the light of the Throne would burn what was there.

At sidrat al-muntahā, the Prophet was near as described by The measure of two bows or closer still (53:9). The report presents a response on behalf of himself and his community to the words of faith in 2:285, followed by God’s assurances in answer to the supplications of 2:286: the community would not be taken to task for forgetfulness or error, would not be overburdened, and would receive pardon, protection, mercy, and help. Imam al-Ṣādiq says that the Prophet requested these things for his community while he was the noblest of God’s visitors. The Prophet was also given the sayings lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā bi-Allāh and lā manjā minka illā ilayka, and was taught a morning and evening supplication seeking refuge in God’s pardon, forgiveness, might, opulence, and eternal Face.

The same narration relates the heavenly adhān, whose clauses God confirmed: God’s greatness, His exclusive divinity, Muḥammad’s messengership, prayer as the obligation owed to Him, and salvation through it. The Prophet led the angels in prayer as he had led the prophets in Jerusalem. Fifty prayers were then imposed on him and his community. Moses repeatedly advised him to seek a reduction because the community could not bear them. After repeated returns and reductions, five daily prayers remained, each counted as ten. The report also states that intending and doing a good deed earns tenfold reward, intending but not doing it earns one reward, doing an evil deed incurs one evil record, and merely intending it without doing it incurs none. Imam al-Ṣādiq closes the report by calling this an exegesis of (17:1).

Al-Mizan notes that similar accounts occur extensively in both Shiʿi and Sunni transmissions. It clarifies some terms in the report: rajulan ādaman means a colored man; ṭāmmah is an overwhelming event; aknāf means sides or zones; the angel whom the Prophet thought might govern worldly affairs was one to whom affairs return; ashmaṭ means hair mixed white and black; zaghab denotes the first small feathers; and ḍabābah means a delicate cloud.

Another report from Imam al-Ṣādiq says that Gabriel carried the Prophet by burāq to Bayt al-Maqdis, showed him the prayer niches of earlier prophets, and returned with him. On the way the Prophet passed a Quraysh caravan searching for a lost camel, drank its water, and poured out the remainder. When he informed Quraysh the next morning, they challenged him to describe Bayt al-Maqdis. Gabriel displayed it before him, enabling him to answer about its pillars, lamps, and prayer niches. The Prophet further foretold that the caravan would arrive at sunrise led by a dusky white camel. Its arrival confirmed the report, including the lost camel and spilled water, but only increased Quraysh’s defiance. Al-Mizan says reports to this effect come from both sects.

A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that Gabriel took the Prophet to the river al-Nūr and instructed him to cross by God’s blessing. Gabriel said that neither a near angel nor a messenger prophet had crossed it, and described angels formed from drops falling from his wings. At the veils Gabriel could proceed no further; the Prophet advanced as God willed, heard that God had derived the name Muḥammad from al-Maḥmūd, and was commanded to announce the honor given him. The same report states that no prophet was sent without a vizier, and that ʿAlī was Muḥammad’s vizier. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Gabriel identified voices heard by the Prophet as those of Pharaoh’s magicians, pilgrims, soldiers, and prophets; at the lote-tree Gabriel again said that he could not advance further. Ibn ʿAbbās also reports the Prophet’s statement that he saw God with his heart rather than his eye.

A report of Imam al-Bāqir answers a question about (43:45) by saying that, at Bayt al-Maqdis, God gathered every prophet and messenger from first to last. Gabriel called the adhān and iqāmah, including “Hasten to the best of deeds,” and Muḥammad led them in prayer. When asked whom they worshipped and what they testified, they professed God’s oneness, Muḥammad’s messengership, and the prior taking of their covenants and oaths upon this.

Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn is reported to have rejected describing God by location. He explains that the Prophet’s ascent was to show him the dominion of the heavens, the wonders God had fashioned there, and the marvels of creation. He interprets the nearness in (53:8-9) as the Messenger’s drawing near to veils of light, seeing the dominion of heaven, then looking down at the dominion of earth.

In another report, Imam al-Bāqir tells Ismāʿīl al-Juʿfī that the journey did not merely end at Bayt al-Maqdis: the Prophet was taken from the Kaʿbah to heaven, with the distance between them a sanctuary. At the farthest lote-tree Gabriel remained behind, saying the Prophet had reached a place no creature had previously reached. The Prophet’s “seeing” of his Lord occurred while the sabḥah stood between them; the Imam explains sabḥah as the majesty of the Lord. In this narration, God taught the Prophet knowledge concerning the dispute in the Highest Council—ranks, expiations, and rewards—and asked who would succeed him. The Prophet named ʿAlī, as the most obedient to him and the most devoted in love to him; God confirmed that ʿAlī was likewise most obedient and loving toward Him. God described ʿAlī as the sign of guidance, leader of His friends, light for those who obey Him, and a lasting word inseparable from the God-fearing; love for ʿAlī is love for God, and hatred for him is hatred for God. God also foretold that ʿAlī would be tested and that others would be tested by him, while granting him four gifts whose ties were in his hand and which he would not disclose.

Al-Mizan explains that the Imam’s phrase “from this to this” means from the Kaʿbah to al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, not that the Farthest Mosque means al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr or that the journey to Bayt al-Maqdis is denied. Extensive traditions identify the Farthest Mosque as Bayt al-Maqdis. “I saw my Lord” means seeing with the eye of the heart, and “the sabḥah blocked between us” means that nothing remained between the Prophet and God except divine majesty. The placing of the hand upon the Prophet’s breast is an allusion to divine mercy and to knowledge revealed directly to his heart so as to remove uncertainty.

A report attributed to the Messenger of God recounts the burāq journey to Bayt al-Maqdis, two rakʿahs of prayer there, and his choice of milk over wine, which Gabriel identifies as fiṭrah. It then gives the successive meetings with Adam; Jesus and John; Joseph; Enoch; Aaron; Moses; and Abraham at al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, visited daily by seventy thousand angels who never return. At the lote-tree, revelation came and fifty prayers were imposed; Moses repeatedly urged reduction until the five prayers remained, each worth ten. A related narration from Anas describes the angels opening the Prophet’s chest and washing it with Zamzam before filling it with belief and wisdom.

Al-Mizan holds that the opening, washing, and filling of the Prophet’s chest describe an imaginal illustration of his spiritual state, not a bodily operation: belief and wisdom are not material things. Narrations of the ascension are full of imaginal illustrations and spiritual metaphors. The narration from Anas suggests both a pre-prophetic occurrence and a dream, but its own account of the imposition and reduction of prayer refutes the claim that the journey occurred before the mission, since prayer could not be imposed before prophethood. Al-Mizan therefore suggests that the angels may first have come before revelation and then returned after the Prophet’s appointment. Its indication that the journey was a dream may, though unlikely, apply only to the chest-opening; apparently, however, it suggests a dream for the entire journey.

Muʿāwiyah b. Abī Sufyān reportedly called the journey a true dream from God, and ʿĀʾishah reportedly said that only the Prophet’s spirit, not his body, was taken. Al-Mizan rejects both views. The plain meaning of (17:1) and the opening verses of Chapter 53, including The eye did not turn aside, nor did it exceed the limit. Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord (53:17-18), do not support a mere dream. The passage praises God’s astonishing mercy and power toward His Prophet, whereas dreams are shared by the righteous and the wicked and are generally regarded as imagination, not proof of power or authority. The report from ʿĀʾishah is additionally discredited by the agreed chronology: the journey occurred in Mecca before the migration, whereas she became the Prophet’s wife after the migration.

Other reports say that Abraham told the Prophet to convey to his community that Paradise has sweet water, good soil, and a wide level land whose seedlings are glorification, praise, profession of divine unity, takbīr, and “There is no movement or might save by God.” Reports from ʿĀʾishah and Imam al-Ṣādiq connect Fāṭimah’s conception and fragrance to fruit from a tree of Paradise or the Ṭūbā Tree eaten by the Prophet during the ascension. Ibn ʿUmar and a report from ʿAlī state that the adhān was revealed and taught to the Prophet on this night.

A narration from Imam al-Kāẓim explains the form of prayer by describing the Prophet’s first prayer before the Throne. He was commanded to wash at the fountain of Ṣād, perform ablution, recite al-Fātiḥah and Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ, bow with glorification of the Magnificent Lord, and prostrate with glorification of the Highest Lord. His second prostration in each rakʿah arose from his own response to the majesty he beheld; God subsequently imposed it as a duty. The prayer initially commanded was two rakʿahs and two prostrations in total, but the Prophet made two prostrations in each rakʿah because of his remembrance of divine greatness. Ṣād is said to be a spring issuing from one of the pillars of the Throne, the water of life, through which God commanded ablution, recitation, and prayer.

Imam al-Ṣādiq is reported to say that the Prophet had two night journeys. In one, Gabriel made him stand where no angel or prophet had stood, and explained God’s ṣalāh as His mercy, expressed by the words that His mercy had preceded His wrath. The Prophet was at the measure of two bows or closer still, with a gleaming veil, said to be of chrysolite, and saw what God willed of the light of His greatness through something like a needle’s eye. Al-Mizan says the opening verses of Chapter 53 support two journeys. It also regards the narration’s explanation of divine ṣalāh as sound: the root sense of ṣalāh is inclination or disposition; God’s inclination is mercy, while the servant’s is supplication. The station where Gabriel stopped signifies the border between creation and the Creator, where divine mercy appears and is effused upon all else; this is the utmost human perfection.

Majmaʿ al-bayān summarizes reports in which Gabriel brought the burāq, the Prophet travelled to Bayt al-Maqdis, prayed there, ascended by a stairway, saw the prophets in successive heavens, and then saw heaven, hell, the Throne, and the lote-tree before returning to Mecca. Quraysh demanded signs, and the Prophet described caravans, lost animals, water vessels, their loads, and the arrival of a caravan led by a dusky white camel at sunrise. Though the signs occurred as foretold, the deniers remained unbelieving.

A report from Imam al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet prayed the Evening and Dawn Prayers in Mecca on the night of the journey; other reports say he prayed the Sunset Prayer there before departing. Al-Mizan finds no contradiction between this and the heavenly imposition of five daily prayers, because prayer itself had already been legislated, though the number of rakʿahs then required is unknown. The Qur’an and hadith show that the Prophet prayed from the beginning of his mission, and he is reported to have led ʿAlī and Khadījah in prayer before his public proclamation.

Imam al-Bāqir is reported to say that the Prophet returned with ten rakʿahs, five two-unit prayers; he later added seven rakʿahs after the births of Ḥasan and Ḥusayn, with God’s permission. He left the Dawn Prayer unchanged because angels of both night and day attend it, and when prayer was reduced on journeys he relieved the community of six rakʿahs but left the Sunset Prayer unchanged. Rules for inadvertence and doubt apply to the part added by the Prophet; doubt in the original prescribed part requires restarting the prayer. Another report from ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn says that after Islam became strong in Medina and jihad was imposed, the Prophet added two rakʿahs each to Noon and Afternoon, one to Sunset, and two to Evening, while leaving Dawn as imposed in Mecca.

Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet smelled the fragrance of Pharaoh’s court hairdresser and her children. Gabriel explained that she confessed belief in God rather than Pharaoh, was cast with her children into a heated copper cauldron, and was strengthened by her suckling child’s miraculous exhortation not to waver because she was upon the truth. Another report says the Prophet saw preachers whose lips were repeatedly cut by scissors of fire because they preached what they did not practice. Al-Mizan identifies such scenes of reward and punishment as imaginal representations (al-tamaththulāt al-barzakhiyyah) of deeds in their consequences and prepared punishments.

The commentary concludes that the traditions on the journey are exceedingly numerous, reaching tawātur, and have been transmitted through many Companions and, in Shiʿi sources, through the Imams. Scholars whose judgment carries weight agree that the journey occurred in Mecca before the migration; reports of the Prophet’s informing Quraysh the following morning, their denial, and the confirming details concerning Bayt al-Maqdis and caravans support this. Reports differ over its year, and Al-Mizan finds no reliable evidence for fixing its date. Traditions from the Imams explicitly state that there were two journeys, and (53:13) may support this; accordingly, particular marvels reported in different accounts may belong to the first journey, the second, or both.

Exegetes also differ over the point of departure: the mountain pass of Abū Ṭālib, Umm Hānī’s house, or the Sacred Mosque itself. Those supporting the first two extend “the Sacred Mosque” to the whole Meccan ḥaram. Al-Mizan holds that the literal meaning is the Sacred Mosque itself and sees no evidence requiring extension or figurative interpretation. If there were two journeys, one may have begun at the Sacred Mosque and the other at Umm Hānī’s house. The mountain-pass account is incompatible with details alleging that Abū Ṭālib and the Hāshimites searched for the Prophet in the Sacred Mosque and threatened Quraysh, since these do not fit their hardship in the mountain pass. In any case, the journey named in (17:1) was from the Sacred Mosque to Bayt al-Maqdis.

On its manner, the majority hold that the Prophet’s body and spirit travelled from the Sacred Mosque to Bayt al-Maqdis and then to heaven. Some hold that body and spirit went to Bayt al-Maqdis but only his spirit ascended thereafter; others reduce the whole event to a true dream. Al-Mizan cites al-Manāqib’s report that the Khārijites denied the ascension, the Jahmiyyah regarded it as a dream of the spirit alone, and the Imamiyyah, Zaydiyyah, and Muʿtazilah affirmed the journey of body and spirit to Bayt al-Maqdis. Others affirm bodily and spiritual ascent to heaven, provided evidence establishes it.

Al-Mizan’s conclusion is that the occurrence of the night journey cannot be denied, since the Qur’an expressly mentions it and recurrent traditions report it from the Prophet and the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt. Verse, narration, context, and circumstances clearly establish that both body and spirit travelled from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque. The ascent to heaven is likewise evident from Chapter 53 and numerous explicit reports. Yet its spiritual character need not mean a dream or a vision in sleep. Such a reading would not make it a sign of divine power and honor, would not explain Quraysh’s vehement denial, and would render the reported events along the way meaningless.

A sound account of spiritual ascent, according to Al-Mizan, is that the Prophet’s noble spirit was taken to a realm beyond matter, inhabited by honored angels, where deeds arrive and divine decrees issue. There he saw the greatest signs of his Lord, the realities of things, the consequences of deeds, the spirits of the greatest prophets, and noble angels. The Throne, veils (al-ḥujub), and pavilions (al-surādiqāt) are divine signs that can only be described metaphorically. Scholars who restrict immaterial existence to God and treat all else as material are led to construe angels, the Throne, the Chair, the Tablet, the Pen, veils, and pavilions as imperceptible material bodies, and to reduce the forms of deeds and their consequences to arbitrary allegory. Al-Mizan judges that this leads to sophistry, including the invalidation of sensory perception and arbitrary links between deeds and their results. Their material view of the spirit also drives those who deny a material ascent to call it a dream, forcing interpretations unsuitable to the verses and narrations.

Majmaʿ al-bayān’s classification of the reports is broadly approved: first, what is certain through knowledge and mass transmission; second, what is rationally possible and does not conflict with established principles, and if it occurred happened while awake; third, what appears to conflict with principles but can be interpreted soundly; and fourth, what appears false and cannot plausibly be interpreted without excessive difficulty, which should not be accepted. The certain core is the journey itself. Reports of traversing the heavens, seeing prophets, the Throne, the lote-tree, heaven, and hell are possible. Reports of people already enjoying heaven or suffering punishment may be interpreted as seeing their attributes or names. Literal claims of seeing God with the physical eye, speaking to Him bodily, or sitting with Him would entail anthropomorphism and must not be taken literally.

Al-Mizan adds that many reports which Majmaʿ al-bayān would treat with difficulty—such as seeing the prophets, the opening and cleansing of the chest, the world appearing as an adorned woman, Jewish and Christian proselytizers appearing as callers, and the depicted rewards and punishments—are imaginal or spiritual representations (tamaththulāt barzakhiyyah aw rūḥiyyah), and therefore pose no problem. The differing forms used for the same reality—ascension on burāq, Gabriel’s wing, or a stairway from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis—further show that these accounts employ imagery and figurative representation. Such imagery in the apparent text of the Qur’an and Sunnah, the commentary concludes, is certain and cannot be denied.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains that “the Book” denotes the comprehensive body of prescribed religious injunctions, including beliefs and practices, by which people settle their differences. Calling it the Book rather than the Torah indicates that its laws were prescribed or written for the Israelites. That God made it guidance explains His giving it to Moses: it set out their Lord’s laws, whose acceptance leads to truth and felicity in both worlds.

The explanatory particle an introduces a summary of the Book’s guidance: “Do not take a protector (wakīlan) besides Me.” It forbids associating anything with God or taking another protector. If the addressed pronoun is the Israelites, this explains the Book’s being their guidance; if it includes Moses, it explains all that precedes.

The shift (iltifāt) from the majestic plural to the singular is required by the monotheistic purport of the command: “protectors besides Us” would not convey it. The majestic plural resumes in the following verse. Taking a wakīl besides God is polytheism, because a wakīl manages the essential affairs and fulfils the needs of the one who appoints him—an office that belongs only to God. Thus taking another lord is equivalent to taking another wakīl.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan holds that dhurriyyah means one’s children, and that its accusative form here marks special attention and supplies a justification for the preceding gift of guidance, just as “surely he was a grateful servant” justifies the description of Noah. God’s special care for the Israelites is thus connected to His earlier promise of peace, blessings, and provision to Noah and those borne with him. Revealing the Book to Moses and making it guidance for the Israelites fulfilled that promise to the descendants of the people of the Ark.

The commentary further explains that the guidance, instruction, and call to monotheism given to Israel continue the custom first undertaken by Noah in the human world. Noah’s gratitude consisted in exclusive worship, since shukr is inseparable from sincere servitude. God rewarded him by preserving his legacy and call, perpetuating praise and peace for him, and rewarding his good words and deeds until the Day of Resurrection: And We made his offspring the survivors. And We perpetuated to him (praise) among the later generations. Peace and salutation to Noah among the nations. Thus do We surely reward the doers of good (37:77-80). The Book was therefore given to Moses as an application of Noah’s enduring way to those borne with him.

From “The offspring of those whom We bore with Noah” (17:3) together with “And We made his offspring the survivors” (37:77), Al-Mizan deduces that all people descend from Noah both maternally and paternally. Were dhurriyyah restricted to his male line, the verse should have said “the offspring of Noah.” Alternative grammatical analyses—taking dhurriyyata as an omitted vocative, as the object of “take,” or as an apposition to Moses—are judged insubstantial. Likewise, the pronoun in “surely he was” is not taken to refer to Moses, nor is “guidance” taken to refer to Moses rather than the Book.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains qaḍaynā as a decisive divine communication: God informed the Israelites through sure revelation in the Book. Qaḍāʾ may denote deciding by word or deed, divinely or humanly; here it is the divine verbal sense of informing and making a definitive ruling.

Although ʿuluww literally means elevation, its conjunction with “make mischief” shows that it here means insolent transgression of limits through wrongdoing and oppression. The verse therefore declares decisively to the Israelites in the Torah that they would commit mischief twice in the land—Palestine and its environs—successively, behaving haughtily and exceeding all bounds.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that “the first of the two” refers to the first of Israel’s two acts of mischief, and that the “promise” is the promised exemplary punishment and vengeance, whose “coming” means the arrival of its fulfilment. The context consequently implies a punishment promised for each act of mischief, though only the first fulfilment is expressly stated here.

God’s sending “Our servants, of mighty prowess (baʾs)” means that He raised and dispatched them to subjugate Israel and exact vengeance. Their going among the houses conveys forcible entry, trampling through the dwellings, and extensive search. The killing, devastation, enslavement, imprisonment, plunder, and destruction they brought were divinely sent as punishment for Israel’s mischief, haughtiness, and unjust transgression; God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.

“We sent” and “Our servants” do not establish that the attackers were believers. God may attribute their action to Himself because it served as punishment, and unbelievers may be called His servants, particularly when described as possessing mighty prowess. The suggestions that they were believers commanded to wage jihād, or unbelievers allied by a prophet against other Israelite unbelievers and sinners, do not alter this point.

The final clause confirms that the declaration was certain and inescapable. The attackers entered by force, penetrated the Israelites’ homes, subjected them, and seized their independence, greatness, and sovereignty.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains al-karrah as a return and nafīr as a band of men that aids and goes forth with a person. The verse apparently means that, after the first punishment, the Israelites would gradually recover rule over their enemies, defeat and overpower them, and be released from enslavement and captivity. Their aid with wealth and children and their becoming a numerous band indicates that this recovery took a considerable time.

In context, the following verse clearly indicates that this renewed ascendancy followed their return to righteousness after experiencing punishment for their first wrongdoing. The second promised punishment likewise followed their return to evil after that restoration.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the lām in li-anfusikum and lahā expresses exclusivity: the good or evil consequence of an act pertains to its doer. The point is responsibility for the result, not merely that good benefits and evil harms its agent. Hence lahā need not be artificially read as ʿalā, as ilā governing isāʾah, or as indicating entitlement to punishment.

This accords with the Qur’anic account of actions: their eschatological consequences never extend beyond the doer. In the world, an action affects another only if God wills it as blessing, punishment, or trial; the agent cannot invariably make its effect reach others. Yet good and evil consequences always reach their doer, who has a share in what he has done. A report from ʿAlī—“You do not do anyone any good or harm”—is cited in this sense.

Li-yasūʾū, derived from masāʾah, means causing grief, and its lām is purposive, with an omitted sense of sending the attackers. They were sent to make sorrow, desolation, subjugation, abjection, and the humiliation of enslavement appear on the Israelites’ faces through massacre, imprisonment, and plunder. The mosque is the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqṣā), Bayt al-Maqdis, not the whole holy land. The verse implies that the attackers had entered it by force on the first occasion as well, though this was omitted there for brevity, and that they entered it to desecrate and destroy it. Apparently, those sent in the second punishment were the same attackers sent the first time.

Tatbīr means utter destruction. The more natural interpretation of “whatever they gained ascendancy over” is that the attackers destroyed what Israel had acquired—through killing, burning property, demolishing buildings, and ruining the land. Although mā may alternatively be infinitival, meaning destruction throughout the period of their ascendancy, the first reading better fits the context. The parallel between the two punishments shows that the second was more severe: the Israelites were nearly exterminated and driven to extinction. Thus, after their second mischief, the attackers were sent to grieve and humiliate them, enter the Farthest Mosque as before, and utterly ruin what they overcame.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains ḥaṣīran as a place of straitening and detention. In context, “It may be that your Lord will have mercy on you” comes after the second dispatch and offers hope of mercy if the Israelites repent and return to obedience and good conduct. “If you again return We too will return” means that if, after mercy and abandoning it, they return to mischief and haughtiness, God will return to punishment and making an example of them. Hell is a prison and place of detention from which unbelievers cannot escape.

The shift from the majestic plural to the third person in “your Lord” indicates what Lordship ordinarily entails: mercy toward servants so long as they follow what their creation and primary nature (fiṭrah) require, rather than deviating from that path. This allusion requires the divine name “Lord”; once it is made, the expression returns to the preceding mode.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that the Qur’an guides to the most upright religion. Aqwam, derived from qiyām, denotes the balanced, effective state of standing and thus metaphorically signifies mastery and sound direction of affairs. The religion is therefore “upright” because it secures human good in both this life and the hereafter, conforms to mankind’s fiṭrah and created capacities, and leads people to their appointed felicity.

If compared with other schools and customs, they may benefit people in some respects while harming them or depriving them in others; Islam alone comprehensively cares for what concerns human life in both worlds. Yet, in light of the preceding discussion of the Torah, “most upright” apparently compares Islam especially with the religions of Noah, Moses, and Jesus. Islam is more complete: it contains divine teaching to the fullest extent human capacity can bear and laws for every individual and social activity. Thus the Qur’an guides more uprightly than earlier Books.

Al-ṣāliḥāt means good deeds. By calling the recompense a “reward,” the verse establishes a promised right for those who believe and do good deeds, a right God has undertaken to fulfill. It declares the promise that will be kept, while the next verse declares the threatened punishment for those who deny the hereafter. A believer who does not do good deeds does not possess this definite claim to reward; his case depends on repentance or intercession, although faith still gives him a firm footing in truth.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains iʿtād as preparing and furnishing something in advance. The verse is apparently conjoined to the preceding promise of reward: the preparation of painful chastisement for deniers of the hereafter is itself good news to believers, since it is divine requital against their enemies in religion.

They are singled out by denial of the hereafter, although they may deny monotheism and prophethood as well, because the discourse concerns the consequence of the upright religion. Religion has neither place nor benefit for one who rejects the hereafter, even if he admits God’s Oneness and other truths. Forgetting the Day of Reckoning is thus the root of every error.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan takes duʿāʾ here to mean every request and pursuit (ṭalab), whether expressed in verbal supplication or pursued through effort. Every such request is in reality directed to God, whether or not the seeker recognizes this, since none but God gives or withholds. Man therefore seeks evil just as he seeks good when, through haste, he pursues whatever first occurs to him or attracts his desire without considering whether it benefits or harms him.

The verse and those following rebuke mankind after the statement that the Qur’an guides to the most upright religion. Although revelation directs people to happiness, Paradise, and every good, man fails to distinguish good from evil, truth from falsehood, happiness from misery, and so rushes toward evil as he rushes toward good. He may not justify this by saying that God enabled him to act and did not prevent him. God’s enabling of both good and evil does not make both permissible.

The differing signs of night and day answer this excuse. Night is faded and obscured, a time of stillness and rest, whereas day is manifest, a time for alert activity, seeking God’s bounty, and reckoning years. Likewise, while both good and bad deeds occur by God’s leave and within the power He grants man, evil must be treated as the obscured sign and avoided; good must be treated as the manifest sign and performed for the happiness and noble provision of the hereafter. A person’s deeds are his inseparable omen and fate: their good or evil returns to their own doer alone.

“Man” means the human genus, not merely unbelievers or polytheists. Good and evil mean what truly produces happiness or wretchedness, not every benefit or harm in an ordinary sense. Haste is love of the immediate attainment of what one desires, not obstinate demands for punishment or calamity.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains mubṣiratan as illuminating or enabling sight. Night and day, the darkness and light that succeed one another over the earth, are in their very being and changing states signs of God; things are not first created without being signs and subsequently made signs. Accordingly, āyat al-layl and āyat al-nahār are the night and day themselves. The passing-away of the night is its darkness, by which it is hidden from sight, while the day is made manifest.

The commentary rejects identifying the two signs with the moon and sun, with the night’s effacement being the moon’s dark spots. The verse speaks of two signs, not two signs belonging to two further signs, and the stated benefits follow from the contrast of daylight and darkness, not from lunar markings. It also rejects the view that night and day simply efface one another, because the verse intends to distinguish the two signs, whereas that reading eliminates their distinction.

The manifest day enables people to seek provision, which is God’s grace, and to calculate years and reckon times and terms. These effects are consequent on the day’s illumination. Though night and day are apparently both used in measuring time, perception first apprehends the existential reality of light; darkness, being lack of light, is known through comparison with it. Al-Rāzī’s interpretation, which makes the night-sign the moon and makes the benefits depend on both signs, does not fit the context.

In context, the verse rebukes man’s hasty pursuit of evil. A person may argue that divine enablement makes any act permissible, but the verse answers that mere ability does not establish permission. Night and day are both divine signs, yet God has assigned night to stillness and rest and day to visibility, livelihood, and reckoning; they are not equally fit for motion and activity. Similarly, God enables both good and evil, but only good is permitted. No one may follow every desire under the pretext of natural freedom and divine enablement.

Thus, although night and day do indicate Divine Unity, that is not their intended function here. The closing statement means that things in creation are distinctly explained, with nothing left ambiguous or unexplained.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains ṭāʾir as that which indicates a person’s good or bad ultimate fortune, and here it means his deeds. The term arose from augury through birds, but the surrounding verses show that a person’s ṭāʾir is what reveals whether his end will be happiness or misery. Its clinging to the neck conveys an attachment inseparable from the person, as the neck itself is inseparable and what is hung upon it is immediately visible.

God has decreed that the actions which bring about each person’s final happiness or misery remain with their doer. Their beneficial or harmful consequences do not depart to another person but return to the actor. Good fate follows faith and God-fearing, while bad fate follows disbelief and disobedience. Thus the verse affirms, rather than denies, that one’s freely acquired good and evil deeds determine one’s end; it rejects the claim that happiness and wretchedness are predestined irrespective of action and obedience.

The book brought forth on the Day of Resurrection is each person’s own book. It contains the full reality of every deed, without omission, and makes its good or evil outcome plainly visible, beyond concealment or excuse. It is not a worldly book of written letters, but the very realities of deeds which the person sees himself; hence its proof is decisive.

Ṭāʾir and book apparently refer to the same deeds. The wording avoids implying either that deeds become a book only at the Resurrection or that the omen was hidden before then, since it already clings to the person. Rather, the book of deeds is presently veiled from human perception by heedlessness, then brought forth in all its detail on the Day of Resurrection. The inevitable consequence of every deed therefore reaches its doer: it clings to him now and appears later as an open book.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that the person will be told to read his own book. The book is incontrovertible evidence, such that even the offender cannot doubt it, because he sees the very deeds that constitute his recompense. He therefore has no valid excuse.

The verse completes the rebuke of human haste. Though God revealed the Qur’an to guide to the most upright religion, man hastens after what he desires without distinguishing good from evil. Yet every good or bad deed remains bound to its doer, is recorded in his book, and will be spread before him on the Day of Resurrection for his own reckoning. Man must therefore reflect before acting, distinguish the good from the evil, pursue the former, and avoid the latter.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan concludes from the attachment of deeds to their doers that guidance benefits its own possessor and error harms its own possessor. No bearer can carry another’s burden in the sense of removing that person’s burden from him. Those who follow erroneous leaders, including those who imitate misguided ancestors, cannot transfer responsibility for their own sins to those leaders.

Leaders of error and founders of evil customs do bear burdens equivalent to those of their followers, but these are burdens arising from their own leadership and innovation. They do not take over the followers’ very sins; otherwise one act would be punished twice as the same burden.

“We have not been chastisers until We raise a messenger” concerns exterminatory punishment in this world, not punishment absolutely or punishment in the hereafter. The wording describes God’s established practice with destroyed nations: He sends a messenger to warn them before their destruction. A messenger (rasūl), unlike a prophet (nabī), holds a special divine position after which decisive judgment comes upon a nation, either through extermination or respite until an appointed term.

The clause qualifies the preceding account of deeds and their consequences. God has the right to punish, but in His mercy and care He does not bring worldly extermination until He has sent a messenger, warned the people, and established proof against them. It negates the occurrence of this punishment before a messenger, not its justification; it does not state a rational principle that punishment without communicated guidance is inherently wrong.

Prophethood communicates duties and clarifies religious law, so otherworldly accountability for practical duties (furūʿ) depends on the prophetic message, since reason alone does not establish their proof. By contrast, reason independently establishes the fundamentals of religion—God’s unity, prophethood, and resurrection—and rejection of these after conclusive rational proof suffices for divine punishment; otherwise the validity of a messenger’s own message would depend circularly on prophethood. Nevertheless, worldly exterminatory punishment follows only the sending of a messenger, by divine care rather than rational necessity.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that the wish to destroy a town means that the time of its destruction has approached, or that the causes required for its destruction have come together—namely, ingratitude for divine bounty and defiant disobedience. Mutrafūn are those living in material abundance and luxury, and tadmīr means utter annihilation.

God does not legislatively command indecency, nor does He existentially command disobedience as disobedience, for such a command would make the act necessary rather than freely chosen and thus no longer disobedience. Two interpretations of the command sent to the affluent are possible. It may be a legislative command to obedience, communicated through a messenger; when they disobey, the word of punishment becomes true against them. Or it may refer to the abundant bestowal of bounty, by which they are granted respite and gradually led on until they actually transgress, after which punishment descends.

The latter is more apparent. In ordinary speech, “I commanded him and he did such-and-such” naturally makes the following action the object of command; moreover, the ensuing transgression belongs to the town as a whole, so there is no evident reason that a command to obey would be restricted to its affluent members. Al-Kashshāf accordingly treats the command as metaphorical: people misuse the bounties meant to enable gratitude, righteousness, generosity, and good works, as though the bounty commanded their transgression. Al-Mizan accepts that this establishes transgression as the apparent object, but not that it excludes the alternative reading. The phrase can also be understood as, “We commanded the affluent to obey, but they disobeyed,” or as an intransitive use of amarnā: God’s command was directed to them, but they transgressed against it.

The suggestion that the phrase merely describes the town rather than supplies the consequence of “when,” and the suggestion that the sentence reverses its proper order so that transgression precedes the wish to destroy, are both rejected as baseless. The common recitation amarnā may also derive from providing abundantly: God gave the affluent abundant wealth and children, then they transgressed. Reported recitations include āmarnā, meaning to provide abundantly or prescribe a duty, and ammarnā, meaning to appoint someone in command.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains qurūn as generations, meaning peoples living in the same time. The verse reinforces the preceding account of God’s practice of destroying towns by recalling the many generations destroyed after Noah. It also hints that this practice belonged to human generations after Noah: before him, human society remained upon its pure fiṭrah, but afterward people diverged from one another.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains al-ʿājilah as the immediate life of this world. To desire it is to make its pleasures and objects the end in themselves, turning away from and forgetting the hereafter; using the world as a means to otherworldly happiness is instead desiring the hereafter. Such exclusive attachment to this world entails denial of the afterlife and effectively annuls attestation to monotheism and prophethood, since religion is futile without resurrection.

God hastens worldly things to such a person, but only what He pleases and only for whom He pleases, not whatever or however much the person wants. At the level of action, God’s effective will consists in the coming together of causes and means; the worldly aspirant receives only as much as the divinely enacted order of causes permits. These causes operate equally for believer and unbeliever: where the causes of wealth are realized, they produce wealth regardless of faith, and where they are absent, wealth is not produced.

The commentary rejects restricting the verse to those who perform religious deeds for worldly gain. This verse states that one whose object is the world obtains nothing beyond it, whereas the cited passage in Chapter 11 concerns receiving in this world the full payment for deeds done for it.

Such a person is then assigned to hell, entering it despised and driven away from divine mercy, wholly deprived of forgiveness and mercy. There are, however, degrees in worldly pursuit and in denial of the hereafter: some pursue the world in practice while justifying it in theory, while others do so outwardly despite inward belief in the hereafter.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that desiring the hereafter means desiring the life after this world, not merely seeking its reward through acts. To strive for it as it deserves is to devote effort exclusively to it and to perform righteous deeds established by incontrovertible reason or legal evidence.

The condition that the person be a believer means correct belief in God, which entails belief in divine unity, prophethood, and resurrection. Since one who seeks the hereafter already believes in God and a life after death, the explicit qualification indicates that this belief must be sound and joined to monotheism and prophethood.

God’s “thanks” for such striving means that He accepts and praises it, bestowing grace upon grace. Reward itself is grace, since the servant’s service to his Master does not independently entitle him to recompense; divine praise in addition to reward is a further grace.

The verse also distinguishes otherworldly from worldly causes. In the hereafter, acts unfailingly attain their end: the striving of one who seeks the hereafter rightly and in faith is surely accepted. Worldly attainment, by contrast, is conditional upon what God pleases and whom He pleases.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains madd and imdād as supplying something with what sustains and extends it, like a stream continuously replenished from its source. God aids both those who desire the immediate life and those who desire the hereafter in all the conditions of their deeds: knowledge, will, bodily faculties, external materials, means, and conditions. These are existential gifts beyond human creation; without God’s bounty, no person can act.

Both groups therefore receive the same divine assistance, but use it differently. One employs God’s bounty in seeking the hereafter and has his striving appreciated; the other uses it for the present life while forgetting the hereafter and is left there with misery and disappointment. Since God’s gifts are blessings suited to righteous use, the transgressor who misuses them has only himself to blame. God remains praiseworthy and possesses the conclusive proof against His servants. The recompense of each group is fitting precisely because all were aided by His pure bounty.

The bounty belongs to “your Lord” because He alone creates and owns what creatures employ. The expression also points to His Lordship, distinguishing the one true Lord from the alleged lords of idolaters. His bounty is not confined: any limitation belongs to the recipient’s capacity and suitability to receive, not to God’s effusion. The commentary therefore rejects the report attributed to al-Ḥasan and Qatādah that limits the bounty here to worldly bounty. The verse concerns the means enabling deeds, not reward; these means comprise both worldly and otherworldly bounty. Even otherworldly bounty is not blocked by a limitation in divine giving, but by the unbeliever’s own unsuitability as recipient.

The verses do not classify every possible mixture of worldly and otherworldly motives or determine the acceptance of every deed. They divide people according to their preferred abode: one either seeks only material prosperity without regard for the other life, or regards the everlasting afterlife as the principal abode and worldly life as preparation for it. Those who seek the hereafter have further cases, such as sinners, innovators, and those lacking faith, but these lie outside the present purpose, which is to distinguish the cause of happiness from the cause of wretchedness.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse points to differing degrees according to differing amounts of striving, so that neither much and little effort nor good and bad action may be thought equal. Worldly superiority includes wealth, prestige, children, power, status, leadership, sovereignty, and popular acceptance.

The hereafter has far greater degrees and preferment than this world. Its differences cannot be measured by worldly differences, because worldly privileges arise from limited material causes in a realm of rivalry and mutual obstruction, whereas otherworldly degrees follow the far greater differences among souls in belief and sincerity, which are states of the heart.

The Prophet is commanded to consider worldly inequalities in order to understand the differing ranks of the hereafter. Different spiritual conditions produce different understandings and intentions, make different actions easy, and ultimately yield different otherworldly degrees.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains khidhlān as the withholding of aid by one expected to help. The verse concludes the preceding account of God’s customary dealing with His servants: those who seek the present life end in hell, despised and neglected, while those who seek the hereafter and strive rightly receive divine appreciation.

Associating another god with God makes one sit down—metaphorically, become humiliated and incapacitated—and prevents one from advancing toward degrees of nearness. Such a person is despised and left without aid from God or from any other helper.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s decree that none be served but Him may be read as negation and exception, prohibition and exception, or the single command to serve Him alone. In every reading, it is a legislative decree (al-qaḍāʾ al-tashrīʿī): a decisive and incontrovertible ruling that can establish prohibitions as well as commands. This wording is more fitting than calling it a mere command, since a command phrased positively would include its prohibition figuratively.

Exclusive, sincere service of God is religion’s greatest command, and associating partners with Him its greatest major sin. All sins ultimately reduce to yielding to something besides God—devils, desire, or ignorance—because ṭāʿah is itself ʿibādah. Even one who denies the Maker is, in this sense, a polytheist: fiṭrah attests to the Creator, while he attributes the ordering of worldly affairs to matter, nature, history, or another such cause. This foundational rule therefore precedes the other prescriptions and is repeated at their conclusion.

Goodness (iḥsān) to parents is the greatest obligatory duty after tawḥīd, while undutifulness to them is among the gravest sins after polytheism. Respect, honor, and kindness toward parents are commanded by fiṭrah and sustain the emotional bonds on which family and society depend; if this practice disappears, children’s attachment to parents and then social ties unravel.

The special mention of parents’ old age concerns their most difficult period, when they need their children’s help after having raised them in their own helplessness. “Ugh” expresses irritation, and nahr is harsh, raised-voice chiding. The verse thus makes honoring parents and treating them with the best conduct incumbent at all times, especially when one or both grow old in the child’s presence.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains khafḍ al-janāḥ as a metaphor requiring the utmost humility, submissiveness, and compassion toward parents in speech and action. It evokes a young bird lowering its wing to seek food from its mother. If dhull is understood as acquiescence (muṭāwaʿah), the image may instead be of a bird lowering its wing to shelter and protect its young compassionately.

The command to pray, “O my Lord! have compassion on them, as they brought me up (when I was) little,” requires remembering their compassionate upbringing and asking God to show them corresponding mercy. Majmaʿ al-bayān infers that a child’s prayer for a deceased parent is heard. Al-Mizan holds only that its answer is possible; even if the parents do not benefit, it is a religious etiquette beneficial to the child. Nothing in the unqualified verse makes the prayer exclusive to deceased parents.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan relates the verse to filial duty and to a child’s impulsive speech or action that harms parents or violates their rights. Such conduct is left unmentioned, as though it is unfitting even to speak of it. God knows what is in people’s minds better than they do; thus, if they are truly characterized by goodness, as He knows from their hearts, He forgives them.

“Those who turn (to Him) frequently” are those who return to God after every disobedience. The verse states this general rule in place of its particular application: when a good child repents after an outburst against his parents, God forgives him.
verses.26: Al-Mizan states that the command to give the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer their due was legislated before the migration, since this is a Meccan verse in a Meccan chapter. Citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, it explains tabdhīr as wasteful, destructive scattering, originally likened to scattering seed. Even a large expenditure is not tabdhīr when it is constructive.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse prohibits squandering because squanderers are the devils’ brothers: not merely followers of their path, but their associates and counterparts, joined as full brothers are by a common root. This understanding is favored over interpreting the phrase simply as the devils’ followers.

“Satan” may mean Iblīs, the father of the devils, or the genus of devils. In either case, Satan is ungrateful because he employs the strength, power, and ability God granted him to lead people into disobedience, sin, and ingratitude. The plural shayāṭīn first indicates that every squanderer is brother to a particular devil; the singular Shayṭān then refers either to Iblīs or to the devilish genus.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan takes the verse to concern someone asked for money. Turning away is not every kind of refusal: it is refusing because one presently has nothing, while striving and hoping for God’s mercy, meaning sustenance. It excludes refusal by a wealthy miser and refusal by one who has nothing and expects no provision. Even then, the requester must be answered gently, without roughness or a dry rejection.

Al-Kashshāf offers two readings of “to seek mercy from your Lord.” It may qualify the command to speak gently: make a beautiful promise that comforts the needy, seeking divine mercy by showing them mercy. Or it may qualify the condition: if one lacks sustenance but hopes God will grant an opening, one should refuse pleasantly; on this reading, mercy means sustenance, and “seeking” means lacking it, with hope mentioned as the effect of that lack.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains the shackled hand as a metaphor for miserly withholding and the hand stretched to its utmost as giving away everything until nothing remains. The verse emphatically prohibits both extremes in giving. “Blamed, stripped off” follows the prohibition of total spending: such giving leaves one blameworthy and cut off from life’s necessities, or naked and unable to meet and deal with people.

Some exegetes make this consequence apply to both withholding and excessive giving, so that miserliness brings blame and excess brings regret. Al-Mizan rejects this reading. The verse does not necessarily prohibit tabdhīr or prodigality here: tabdhīr is improper expenditure, whereas spending much or even all one’s property in God’s way and on deserving recipients need not be improper or regrettable. Nevertheless, giving everything is prohibited because it leaves the giver without means.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as the reason for forbidding the two extremes in giving. God’s established way is to expand sustenance for whomever He wills and to contract it for whomever He wills, according to His servants’ welfare; He neither expands it without limit nor withholds it altogether. Since He is Aware of and Seeing His servants, people should adopt this divine manner by maintaining moderation.

Some exegetes instead say that the verse means the expansion and restriction of provision belong exclusively to God, so people should not assume that affair but keep balance. Al-Mizan considers this and other proposed explanations unlikely.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains al-imlāq as poverty and need, and khiṭʾan as a grave, intentional wrong rather than a mere mistake. The verse severely forbids killing children from fear of poverty: God, not parents, sustains both the children and the parents, so such fear cannot justify killing them. It is a specially emphasized form of killing an innocent soul, marked by extreme hardheartedness; frequent famine and drought may have contributed to its particular prevalence among the Arabs.

Al-Kashshāf identifies the children here with daughters buried alive. Al-Mizan finds this apparently incorrect. Other verses explicitly address burying daughters to escape disgrace, whereas this verse speaks of poverty, not disgrace, and “children” gives no reason to restrict its scope to girls. It prohibits a distinct evil custom: killing sons or daughters from fear of poverty and need.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan holds that the command not even to approach adultery is an intensified prohibition. Adultery is inseparably an indecency and an evil way because it corrupts society: it loosens social bonds, disturbs order, corrupts lineages, cuts off progeny, brings sexually transmitted diseases and crimes, and erodes chastity, modesty, ghayrah, kindness, and mercy. The Qur’an consequently threatens its perpetrator severely, while making an exception for repentance, faith, and righteous action (25:68-70).

The commentary argues that sexual attraction and the corresponding faculties are naturally directed to reproduction and the preservation of the species. In animals, this entails mating and care for offspring. Human marriage, likewise, has historically been an exclusive bond between man and woman, satisfying instinct and producing children; households are the basis from which human societies arose. Marriage’s exclusivity gives rise to ghayrah, protective jealousy, distinct from ḥasad and shuḥ.

Accordingly, marriage has generally been praised and adultery condemned, apart from instances reported among some savage tribes. Al-Mizan says that modern Western civilization instead gives individual material enjoyment and freedom priority over religious, ethical, and ethnic norms so long as secular law and consent are not infringed. It attributes to this orientation the spread of extramarital relations, including among married people and in incest; the growth of children born out of wedlock; and the decline or ridicule of chastity, modesty, and protective jealousy.

The commentary says divine religions strongly prohibit adultery: Judaism made it unlawful, and its unlawfulness can be inferred from the Gospels. Islam treats it as a major sin, more gravely in incestuous cases and when committed by a married person, and sets severe penalties: 100 lashes for up to two or three times, followed by death for the third or fourth offence for unmarried persons, and stoning to death on the first offence for married persons.

“An evil way” apparently means the way of subsistence: sexual union with women is the means of the human race’s continuance, and the marital family is the strongest instrument for preserving civic society. Once adultery offers an easy satisfaction of instinct, marriage loses attraction because its remaining features are its financial, bodily, and child-rearing burdens. Al-Mizan says this reduces marriage in Western societies to a fragile partnership in secondary affairs, treating shared life as its end and reproduction, children, and sexual satisfaction as merely optional consequences. This departs from creation, whose immediate aim in mating is instinctual satisfaction and whose longer aim is offspring. If partnership for material needs were marriage’s purpose, partnerships of two men or two women should have become prevalent in human history.

The commentary further maintains that children born out of wedlock weaken paternal love, compassion, and attachment, leading to abandonment of marriage and eventually social extinction. It rejects the expectation that mechanical or scientific means, including incentives for procreation, can preserve society without natural instincts: social institutions endure only when rooted in and accepted through human natural faculties. To oppose those instincts and neglect their primary ends threatens humankind’s extinction, even if its full result is not yet apparent. In Islamic law, adultery also confuses lineages, on which marriage and inheritance laws depend.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse forbids killing an innocent soul, except where the shariah establishes a just cause, such as murder, apostasy, or other specified acts. Since al-nafs is unqualified by Islam or monotheism, the verse may indicate a universal prohibition of killing any human being, found in all divine laws.

When someone is slain unjustly, his heir, as guardian (walī) over his blood, is given legal authority to retaliate against the murderer, take blood-money, or pardon. The heir must not exceed the limits by killing anyone other than the murderer or by killing more than one person. He is “aided” through this legal authority, which ensures that the murderer will not escape; nor should that divine aid lead him to exceed.

Some exegetes refer “let him not exceed” to the murderer and “he is aided” to the slain person, making the verse a warning not to kill unjustly because the victim’s heir will be empowered. Al-Mizan judges this unlikely in light of the verse’s context and pronouns.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that the command not even to draw near to an orphan’s property emphatically forbids consuming it unjustly, a major sin threatened with fire. The exception for a goodly way permits only what best protects and constructively develops the property. The limit “till he attains his maturity,” meaning puberty and adulthood, shows that the duty is to preserve the orphan’s property and return it once he is no longer an orphan.

Every promise will be questioned about—that is, people will be questioned concerning it. Some hold that the promise itself will be questioned, since deeds may be embodied on the Day of Resurrection to testify, intercede, or oppose people.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains qisṭās as a scale, and the true balance as one that is just and does not diminish weights. Full measure and just weighing are khayr because they prevent the concealed theft of people’s property and win their trust. They are better in the end, taʾwīlan, because sound economic life depends both on obtaining useful goods and exchanging one’s surplus for what one needs.

Fraudulent measures and unjust balances damage both sides of people’s economic life and cause trust and security to disappear. Just measures instead enable correct calculation of livelihoods, improve economic conditions, establish trust between people and merchants, and spread security.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan holds that “And follow not that of which you have not any knowledge” is unconditional: it forbids adopting an ungrounded belief, utterance, or action. It confirms fiṭrah, by which human beings seek reality in belief and right action in practice. A person may follow an expert—such as a guide, doctor, or specialist—only because he knows that person possesses the relevant knowledge and competence. Thus such reliance ultimately remains a following of knowledge, although people sometimes mistake what merely satisfies their souls for certain knowledge.

Accordingly, where direct knowledge can be acquired, one may not adopt a belief or practice before acquiring it. Where it cannot readily be acquired, one may act only upon knowledge of a proof that warrants the act. Following a prophet’s religious law rests on knowledge of his infallibility, and following a doctor or specialist rests on knowledge of their expertise. Even when a knowledge-based proof directs one to act on presumptive evidence, the act is still, in reality, a following of knowledge.

This resolves the objection associated with Rāzī that the verse cannot universally forbid speculation, since religious branches often use presumptive evidence and the verse’s own apparent meaning is presumptive. Al-Mizan replies that acting on presumptive evidence in such cases follows a binding proof grounded in knowledge, not speculation as such; therefore no exception to the verse is needed. Likewise, accepting a text’s apparent meaning is warranted by the binding rational practice of treating apparent meanings as proof, so the verse does not negate itself.

The hearing, sight, and heart will themselves be questioned and testify for or against the person. The pronouns most naturally refer to these faculties, not to the person who follows without knowledge; the latter interpretation is unlikely given the shift from second to third person. Hearing, sight, and heart are the God-given instruments by which truth is acquired, and the heart here is the faculty of understanding and comprehension. Each will be asked whether it sought certainty and whether the person followed the knowledge obtained through it; no excuse will then be accepted. The verse thus resembles passages in which bodily parts testify, while distinctively including the soul’s own understanding as a witness.

Majmaʿ al-bayān reports interpretations restricting the first clause to falsely claiming to have heard, seen, or known something; to backbiting; or to false witness. It also calls the verse universal over every speech, act, and decision not based on knowledge. Al-Mizan accepts the universality but qualifies its formulation: the verse says not to follow when one lacks knowledge, not that one may follow only when one knows an act is permissible. The reported applications are better treated as examples of the verse’s concluding rationale.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains maraḥ as intense, invalid joy that exceeds balance, weakens the intellect, and manifests in conduct, speech, and especially one’s gait. Valid joy is gratitude for God’s blessing within proper limits. The prohibition of walking exultingly therefore forbids vainglory, insolence, pride, and conceit, which appear particularly in the way one walks.

The statement that one cannot cut through the earth or reach the mountains in height metaphorically exposes arrogant displays of power and greatness as imagined illusions: the earth is stronger than one’s steps and the mountains taller than oneself. Property, honor, dominion, power, supremacy, and wealth likewise have no reality beyond the human mind. Yet God has formed souls to recognize and employ these imagined matters so that worldly life may be built and His decree fulfilled; without them, human beings could not live in the world.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that the verse refers back to all the preceding commands and prohibitions. The evil, forbidden matters among them are hateful to God: He neither approves of them nor is pleased with them. An uncommon reading, sayyiʾatan rather than sayyiʾuhu, simply makes the meaning that all the preceding matters are evil and hateful to the Lord.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains “This” as all the detailed prescriptions just given. They are called wisdom even though they are legal injunctions, because their expediencies can be inferred from the preceding verses. The renewed prohibition of associating another god with Allah, and its warning of being cast into hell blamed and rejected, emphasizes the supreme importance of monotheism and joins the conclusion of the passage to its beginning.
verses.40: Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question negates the claim that angels are God’s daughters. Iṣfāʾ means choosing and singling out; thus the claim absurdly assigns God the females whom the audience regarded as abject while granting themselves sons, although He is their Lord and the director of all things. “Females” (ināthan), rather than daughters (banāt), perhaps reflects their contempt for femininity generally. This is a grievous saying with evil consequences.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that taṣrīf is the abundant variation and repetition of expression, while nufūr is turning away from something. The Qur’an repeatedly and variously sets out arguments for monotheism and against polytheism so that people may remember and the truth may be clear; yet each renewed expression increases these people’s aversion. The shift from directly addressing them to speaking of them shows that, through this attitude, they are unworthy of direct address.

Majmaʿ al-bayān holds that revelation remains wise despite their increased aversion because it completes the proof against them, guides others who would otherwise not be guided, and, it claims, prevents a greater evil. Al-Mizan rejects the last claim: increased aversion produces denial, opposition, and obstruction of truth, than which there is no greater evil for religion’s propagation. Nevertheless, disbelief and hostility destroy their own possessors while serving the believers who accept and submit to truth; without their opposites, good traits and virtues would not be realized. Wisdom therefore requires proofs to be supplied fully, bringing the wretched to the utmost realization of their wretched capacity and raising the felicitous through their contrasting deeds, as in: All do We aid—these as well as those—out of the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20).
verses.42:
Al-Mizan says that the verse addresses, through the Prophet, the polytheists’ belief in subordinate gods who govern distinct domains. Partnership in directing affairs entails sovereignty (mulk), and sovereignty over a thing follows from creating it; even they acknowledge God as the sole Creator. Their claim therefore supposes that His sovereignty and lordship can be divided.

If other gods could possess any part of the sovereignty that proceeds from God’s Essence, their innate love of dominion would make them seek to overcome the Lord of the Throne, seize His kingdom, and rule alone. “Seeking a way to the Lord of the Throne” means seeking access to His Throne in order to take His sovereignty, not seeking nearness to Him. The latter reading, attributed to some early exegetes, does not fit the designation “Lord of the Throne” or the following exaltation of God: the dreadful implication being denied is that His sovereignty could be approached, contested, transferred, or usurped.

The commentary also rejects equating this argument with If there had been in them any gods except Allah, they would both have certainly been in a state of disorder (21:22). That verse argues from the disorder resulting from multiple governing powers, whereas this verse argues that alleged partners would seek to overthrow God and seize His dominion. The former is instead akin to In that case would each god have certainly taken away what he created, and some of them would certainly have overpowered others (23:91).
verses.43: Al-Mizan explains that taʿālā denotes the utmost exaltation, reinforced by “high” (kabīran). The verse declares God utterly exalted above the polytheists’ assertion of other gods and the implication that His sovereignty and lordship could be disputed or captured.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse, together with the preceding glorification, both exalts God and completes the argument against polytheism. If there were gods besides Him, they would seek to overcome Him and seize His kingdom; but the heavens, earth, and all within them glorify Him and testify that His kingdom originates from, subsists through, and returns to no one but Him. Their utter dependence on Him means that none can possess sovereignty or lordship besides Him.

Tasbīḥ is declaring purity through speech, and speech in its essential sense is any disclosure of what is intended, not merely audible human words. A thing whose very constitution discloses a meaning thus speaks by its being. All existents disclose their Lord’s oneness and freedom from imperfection: in themselves they are pure need and deficiency, dependent on Him in essence, attributes, and states, and so point to the All-Sufficient, perfect Existantiator (al-Mūjid). Their interrelated perfections and the unified system encompassing them further disclose that their one Lord directs all affairs and fulfils every need. Even a polytheist’s conception, utterance, and means of expressing denial, being needy existents, testify against that denial, like someone verbally claiming that no one can speak.

The commentary rejects treating this glorification as metaphorical. The Qur’an indicates that knowledge accompanies creation, each being having knowledge according to its share of existence, though not necessarily human-like or intelligible to human beings. Every created thing therefore consciously expresses its need, which is met by its one Lord, and literally glorifies Him. This real, spoken glorification (qālī) need not be verbal sound. The view that angels and believers glorify literally while inanimate things do so only by their state is likewise weak; a metaphorical reading is warranted only where the literal is impossible. The wording, “but you do not understand their glorification,” confirms this, since people do understand that things are signs of their Creator, whereas the verse negates understanding of their actual glorification. Interpretations that reduce this to failure to reflect, or to incomplete understanding expressed by generalization, neither suit the argument nor the Qur’an’s precision.

Everything also praises God (ḥamd). Its need and imperfection declare His freedom from need and defect, while the existence, blessings, and perfections bestowed on it disclose His beautiful attributes and actions. Considered without regard to creatures’ cognition, these disclosures are simply signs (āyāt) of God; but their glorification and praise themselves are real. Reports through both Shiʿa and Sunni chains concerning objects’ glorification accord with this understanding.

Finally, God’s being Forbearing and Forgiving means that He does not hasten punishment and forgives the repentant. His forbearance implies no fear of losing the chance to avenge, and His forgiveness no loss through mercy; both demonstrate that His sovereignty cannot be diminished. The commentary calls it a fine point that these attributes may also concern humanity’s failure to understand the constant glorification of all things: people deserve punishment for this deficiency, but He grants respite and may forgive, implying that such understanding lies within human capacity.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan apparently takes the “hidden barrier” to be a spiritual barrier, imperceptible to the senses, placed between the Prophet as reciter and bearer of the Qur’an and polytheists who deny the hereafter.
