It prevents them from grasping the Qur’an’s reality, believing in the Prophet and his true messengership, or accepting God’s oneness and the hereafter; hence they turn away at the mention of God alone, persist in denying resurrection, and call him bewitched. Their description as deniers of the hereafter is apt because that denial voids belief in divine unity and messengership and thus entails unbelief in all fundamental religious beliefs.

The commentary notes grammatical proposals that mastūran may mean characterized by concealing or even “veiling,” as well as the suggestion that the concealed thing is what lies behind the barrier. It regards as least likely the explanations that words are omitted, that one barrier is hidden by another, or that the barrier is unknown as a barrier and they are ignorant of their ignorance.
verses.46: Al-Mizan explains the coverings on their hearts and heaviness in their ears as the hidden barrier of the preceding verse: their hearts are veiled from understanding the Qur’an, and their ears are burdened so that they neither listen submissively nor understand with conviction and acceptance. This is punishment for their disbelief and wrongdoing. When the Qur’an proclaims their Lord alone—affirming monotheism and negating polytheism—they turn away in aversion and shirk.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as justifying the claim that coverings have been placed on the polytheists’ hearts and heaviness in their ears. God knows best the ears with which they listen to the Prophet and the hearts with which they secretly deliberate, since He created and directs these faculties; His report of their condition is therefore supremely true. Their whispered statement, “You follow only a man bewitched,” is itself an unjust utterance showing that they have not recognized the truth.

The verse explicitly indicates that they did not openly come to hear the Qur’an, fearing one another’s blame. They came furtively and, when they encountered one another, reproached each other in whispers lest the Prophet and believers discover them. This reading accords with the reported circumstances of revelation mentioned later.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains mathāl as a description, so ḍarb al-amthāl means describing a person’s attributes and characteristics. Their descriptions of the Prophet show that they have gone astray and cannot find the way; the verse implies that there is no hope of their faith.
verses.49: Al-Mizan explains rufāt as debris or matter broken down and ground into powder. The polytheists’ question continues their failure to understand the Qur’an by expressing doubt about resurrection, a central truth established by revelation and intellect, though they offer no argument against it beyond its seeming improbability. They imagine death to be annihilation and therefore regard the creation of a human being anew after bones have crumbled into particles as generation from sheer nothingness. The following answer recalls God’s absolute power and their first creation.
verses.50: Al-Mizan says that the command to become stones, iron, or anything still harder to receive life answers their doubt about resurrection. Since these seem even less capable than powdered bones of becoming human, the challenge shows that God’s absolute power is not limited by what material they become. Whatever they choose to be, He can restore their initial human creation and resurrect them.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that when the deniers ask who will restore them, the answer, “He Who created you at first,” removes the supposed impossibility of return by citing their first creation from nothing as its precedent. Naming God by this description rather than by the majestic name proves His power to restore them.

Their shaking of their heads is derisive surprise and contempt after this argument, as they ask when resurrection will occur. “Maybe it has drawn nigh” does not fix its time, for that belongs to the hidden (ghayb) known only to God; instead, the following verse describes the Day itself, when they will be summoned and respond in praise.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains God’s call as His command to rise for the Day of Judgment and their response as their acceptance of that call. They will respond in a state of praising Him, recognizing resurrection and their return as a praiseworthy divine act, because then they will see that divine wisdom requires resurrection for reckoning and a second realm after the first.

They will think that they remained in their graves only a little while, realizing how near the Day truly was. God confirms the brevity of their stay while rejecting the particular periods they may suppose. This answers their present mockery of resurrection as distant and unlikely: on that Day they will regard it as near and will praise the very return they now deride.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan takes “My servants” to mean the believers, an honorary attribution, and “that which is best” to mean speech marked by good manners and free of harshness, abuse, and every evil. The Prophet is commanded to command them thus because Satan sows dissension among people and is humanity’s manifest enemy.

Together with the following verses, this directs believers to good speech and proper manners rather than presuming to declare who is felicitous or doomed, or relying on the Prophet’s following as a guarantee of salvation. The Prophet cannot waive obligations, grant or withhold good at will, or pronounce evil upon people; goodness of heart and excellence of speech are what remain. David’s Psalms accordingly exemplify excellent speech and God’s glorification.

The passage indicates that before the migration believers spoke with polytheists and sometimes answered harshly—perhaps saying that believers would enter Paradise and their opponents Hell. Such speech inflamed hostility, worsened the believers’ persecution, harmed the Prophet, and intensified resistance to truth. The command also fits the preceding insults against the Prophet and ridicule of the Qur’an. Although some interpret it as a Meccan prohibition on fighting and an order to treat polytheists peacefully, Al-Mizan says that the stated rationale about Satanic dissension does not support that interpretation.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan connects this verse to the preceding command of good speech. Whether its first part addresses believers through the Prophet or addresses both directly, it gives a further reason not to speak harshly or judge particular people as felicitous, damned, destined for Paradise, or destined for Hell. Their Lord knows them best and judges, according to His knowledge, who merits mercy and who merits chastisement.

His willing mercy is not apart from belief and righteous deeds, and His willing chastisement is not apart from disbelief and sin. The Prophet has not been sent as one in charge of people’s affairs, able to decide whom to give or withhold from as he pleases. Thus believers must not rely upon the Prophet or their mere identity as his followers for salvation; recompense follows faith, righteous action, evil, disbelief, and sin.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains that God’s complete knowledge of those in the heavens and earth confirms that He knows human beings best. The preference of some prophets over others prepares for the special mention of David: the Psalms demonstrate his excellence through their supreme glorification and praise of God, while encouraging believers toward good speech and proper manners in conversation.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan notes that zaʿm, though it can denote any belief, is ordinarily used for a false belief; Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that whatever the Qur’an calls zaʿm is a lie. Duʿāʾ is broader than nidāʾ: the latter is a vocal call, whereas the former may also occur by gesture or other communication.

The verse refutes worship of other-than-God on the principle that a true lord must independently confer benefit and avert harm. The polytheists themselves worship their alleged gods in hope of benefit and fear of harm, yet call upon them in distress when they can neither remove it nor transfer it. Those invoked—including angels, jinn, and human beings—are creatures who seek nearness to God, hope for His mercy, and fear His chastisement. Idols themselves have no reality beyond names given by people: wood and metal images are inanimate objects, while their worship was meant to seek proximity to the beings or spiritual realities they represented.

The commentary holds that the verse denies independent control, not every form of creaturely power. God has ascribed powers to angels, jinn, and mankind, but “The power is wholly God’s” (2:165): whatever power or ownership creatures possess is conferred, loaned, and effective only by His permission and will. Thus the verse does not support the Ashʿarite claim that contingent beings have no power whatsoever. The objects of worship are like their worshippers in dependence upon God; a request addressed to one whose power belongs to another is, in reality, directed to the independent Owner of that power.

One exegete accordingly limits the denial to complete power to remove distress, observing that there is no decisive proof that angels and jinn have absolutely no such power. Nor can one simply argue that false gods fail to answer while God always grants requests, since Muslims’ requests may also appear unfulfilled. Al-Mizan answers that God says, “I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he calls on Me” (2:186) and “Call upon Me, I will answer you” (40:60). A call made sincerely, seriously, and with a heart detached from all other-than-God is certainly answered. In sea-distress, people are cut off from other means and, guided by fiṭrah, call upon God alone; He rescues them. False gods cannot answer when the caller is similarly cut off from God and calls them alone.

A translator’s note qualifies that God’s answering of duʿāʾ is not identical with granting every suʾāl: divine wisdom and the trial of this world govern how the answer appears. This does not alter the contrast in the verse, which is between the polytheists’ unanswered invocation of their gods and their own sincere invocation of God in sea-distress, not between false worship and ordinary Muslim requests. The command, “Say,” also enables the Prophet himself to meet the objection by calling on his Lord with this sincere detachment, a call that would certainly be answered.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan takes al-wasīlata more plausibly to mean the means by which one approaches God, rather than merely the act of approaching Him. Those whom the polytheists invoke—including angels, jinn, and human beings—are themselves seeking the means of nearness to their Lord. They look to whoever among them is nearest to God so as to follow his path and deeds, hope for God’s mercy in every aspect in which they depend on Him, and fear His chastisement; therefore they obey rather than disobey Him.

Seeking nearness to God through those near to Him resembles the command, “O you who believe! be careful of (your duty to) Allah and seek means of nearness to Him” (5:35). It differs fundamentally from polytheism. The polytheists began by seeking God through noble angels, jinn, and righteous human beings, but then abandoned worship, hope, and fear of God for worship, hope, and fear directed to those means. They then made idols and images means to those beings, and eventually worshipped the idols themselves through offerings and sacrifices. By treating these creatures or images as independent in lordship and worship, they made them God’s partners.

If the invoked beings include rebellious devils or sinful humans as well as righteous beings, their seeking, hope, and fear refer to their existential subservience, glorification, hope, and fear. The commentary rejects the view that all the plural pronouns refer instead to prophets who call people to God or petition Him, since this does not suit the context. Al-Kashshāf’s readings—that even the nearest of their gods seeks nearness to God, or that they eagerly seek closeness through obedience and good deeds—are not intrinsically objectionable, though the second better fits the context. The further claim that each alleged god strives by worship to become nearest to God is not supported by the wording of the verse.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan reports an interpretation in which “destroy” means the natural death of a town’s inhabitants and “severe chastisement” an exterminating punishment, since every town will perish when the world ends; on this view, destruction concerns righteous towns and chastisement unrighteous ones. It judges, however, that the verse apparently returns to “And when We wish to destroy a town, We send Our commandment to the affluent ones, so they transgress therein; thus the word proves true against it, so We destroy it with utter destruction” (17:16). The passage belongs to the Qur’an’s account of God’s constant way: He calls people to truth, grants felicity to those who obey, and chastises those who arrogantly transgress.

Accordingly, “destroy” means extermination, as reported from Abū Muslim, while “severe chastisement” means lesser but grave punishments—such as famine, dearth, or disasters that force migration or ruin a town’s infrastructure. Towns meet this fate through their people’s corruption and the transgression of their affluent ones (mutrafūn). This also explains the following verse: the present polytheists share the ancient deniers’ disposition to reject divine communications. Were tremendous requested signs sent to them, their rejection would entail destruction as it did for earlier nations. God grants them respite rather than hastening this end, though it will ultimately reach them. The claim that “town” refers only to unbelieving towns has no proof.

The destruction or chastisement is a certain decree written in al-kitāb, identified here with the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), in which the Qur’an says everything is recorded. Al-Mizan rejects discussions that treat this Tablet as a physical object containing detailed descriptions of all things. A finite material tablet could not contain even the exhaustive details of its own components, much less all beings, events, and relations; limiting the verse to one realm does not solve the difficulty. Nor does comparing the Tablet to letters that potentially contain infinitely many words suffice, since the Qur’anic description concerns all past, present, and future things as actualized, differentiated, and fixed by unchanging necessity. Moreover, what is material is changeable, whereas maḥfūẓ means preserved from every conceivable change.

The commentary concludes that the Clear Book (al-kitāb al-mubīn) is the very “text” of existents and their events at the level where an effect necessarily follows its cause. It is the unchanging divine decree (qaḍāʾ), not the potentiality and contingency proper to matter. “Book” and “Tablet” are symbolic expressions that make this reality intelligible.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s withholding of the requested signs follows His decree concerning towns: ancient peoples received such signs, rejected them, and were consequently destroyed. The present generation has the same disposition as its predecessors; if its demanded signs were sent, it too would reject them and incur exterminating punishment. God does not wish to hasten its punishment, though these verses are connected with the demands later reported in “And they say: We will by no means believe in you until you cause a fountain to gush forth from the earth for us” (17:90).

The ancient rejection did not literally restrain God, for none can repel His judgment. Rather, because rejection would make the sending of proposed signs devoid of welfare or wisdom for a people whom God has not willed immediately to destroy, it is figuratively described as a hindrance. Alternatively, the language points to later people following the same path as the former while God has decreed respite for this nation. The use of irsāl, “sending,” may suggest that signs are ready to descend but are withheld only because of the people’s rejection and corruption. Calling the destroyed peoples al-awwalūn further suggests one continuing nation: its last members have the same makeup as its first, so what befell the former applies to the latter.

Other interpretations reduce to this meaning: proposed signs are not sent because they would be futile when God knows they will not be believed, except where a sign is needed to establish a messenger’s mission or is sent as divine grace; or the present people merely imitate their ancestors, who asked for comparable signs and then disbelieved. Thamūd, the tribe of Prophet Ṣāliḥ, was given the she-camel as a clear, manifest sign, yet wronged themselves by rejecting it.

Signs are sent to warn and make people fear. Signs that entail extermination warn of worldly chastisement, while other signs warn of the Hereafter. Al-Mizan also considers likely that the intended signs are frightening but non-exterminating catastrophes, sent so that people may guard themselves against a more dreadful punishment rather than be immediately annihilated.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan observes that the verse’s four clauses are connected only elliptically. The Qur’an does not elsewhere identify the Prophet’s vision, and the visions in 8:43 and (48:27) concern post-migration events, whereas this verse was revealed in Mecca. Nor does the Qur’an explicitly call the Zaqqūm tree cursed. Though it calls Zaqqūm a trial, its growing in Hell and serving as punishment cannot itself make it cursed; otherwise Hell, its punishments, and its obedient angels of chastisement would likewise be cursed.

The context instead gives a general indication. It follows the account of recurrent rejection, corruption, and punishment among human societies and precedes the account of Iblīs’s misguidance of Adam’s descendants. Thus the vision and the cursed tree concern a past or future human affair that tests people, breeds corruption, and entrenches defiance. “Your Lord encompasses men” means His knowledge encompasses them: He knows that people will persist in the inherited course of sin and disregard of His signs. His warnings, whether verbal admonitions or frightening non-exterminating events, do not restrain them but increase their great insolence. The verse consoles the Prophet by presenting these affairs as part of God’s continuing trial of His servants.

Since the tree is cursed “in the Qur’an,” its curse must belong among the Qur’an’s curses. Shajarah can mean not only a plant but a root that branches, such as a pedigree or the followers of a belief. The relevant cursed group must therefore grow and branch within the ummah, whether through descent or through a corrupt doctrine inherited by later generations, and become a trial of misguidance. Of the possible Qur’anic groups—the followers of the Book, polytheists, and hypocrites—the first two do not fit, since Muslims were assured near the end of the Prophet’s life that the disbelievers had despaired of harming their religion: “This day have those who disbelieve despaired of your religion, so fear them not, and fear Me” (5:3). The commentary concludes that the tree is a group of hypocrites who outwardly enter Islam, establish themselves in the community, and become a trial. The linked clauses further imply that God showed the Prophet this tree and some of its actions in Islam in a dream.

Al-Mizan says this conclusion is confirmed by reports in some Sunni sources and unanimously from the Ahl al-Bayt: the vision concerned the Umayyads, and the tree was their pedigree. It rejects the interpretation, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, that the vision was the night journey and the tree Zaqqūm. Ruʾyā lexically denotes a dream, and the suggested attempts to make it a waking vision, anything seen at night, an expression based on the polytheists’ assumption, or a metaphor lack linguistic or contextual evidence. The claim that the night journey itself was a dream has already been rejected in the commentary’s discussion of the chapter’s opening.

It also rejects the proposed explanations of Zaqqūm’s curse. Cursing the tree as a metonymy for those who eat from it is unsuitable to the Qur’an’s manner; laʿn means distance from mercy and good, not mere distance in an unrestricted sense; and if Zaqqūm were cursed because it is far from mercy in Hell, Hell, its punishments, and its guardian angels would have to be cursed as well. Resemblance of its spathes to devils’ heads and the claim that harmful food is called cursed likewise require unsupported metaphorical shifts. Even if Ibn ʿAbbās’s report were sound, it is not an authoritative proof (ḥujjah), especially against reports containing the Prophet’s interpretation.

Al-Kashshāf avoids the night-journey reading by connecting the vision to a supposed pre-Badr dream of Quraysh’s defeat and their falling places, and connects Zaqqūm to Quraysh’s ridicule of a tree in Hell. Al-Mizan rejects this as an unproved speculation resting only on “perhaps.” The interpretation that the vision was the Prophet’s entry into Mecca is chronologically impossible, because that vision occurred after the migration. Abū Muslim’s suggestion that the tree means the Jews has some support insofar as they are cursed and can be called a tree, but it is weakened by the assurance of 5:3 that they would no longer be a threatening trial to Muslims.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan treats the grammatical discussions of ṭīnan as yielding the sense that Adam was created of or from clay. The verse recalls Iblīs’s refusal of the command to prostrate to Adam. His question is a disapproving rhetorical question: he refuses to prostrate to one created of clay, implicitly contrasting Adam with himself, who was created from fire and whom he regards as nobler.

The reminder confirms the preceding account of people’s persistent disparagement of God’s commands, rejection of truth, and neglect of His signs. The Qur’an gives only an abridged form of the story because the context concerns the forces that make Adam’s descendants persist in sin and injustice. It recalls Iblīs’s pledge to mislead them, his request for authority over them, and God’s granting him authority over those who themselves deviate and follow Satan and his cavalry and infantry, while God’s chosen servants are excluded. In view of divine tribulation on one side and Satan’s forces on the other, the prevalence of error, transgression, and departure from God’s signs is not surprising.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains that “this he whom You have honored above me” refers to Adam, whom God preferred over Iblīs by commanding Iblīs to prostrate to him and driving Iblīs away when he refused. Iblīs inferred Adam’s honor from this command, and this stirred his resolve to mislead Adam’s descendants.

Iḥtināk originally conveys taking something completely, as locusts consume an entire field; its underlying image is apparently fastening a rope to an animal’s lower jaw and drawing it. It therefore means bridling. Having incurred divine wrath, Iblīs swears that, if granted respite until the Day of Resurrection—the span of humanity’s earthly life—he will bridle Adam’s progeny, except for a few: God’s chosen servants (al-mukhlaṣūn).
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that “Be gone” is not primarily a command but a dismissal, like saying to an opponent, “Do whatever you want.” Some exegetes take it as an actual command equivalent to “Then get out of it, for surely you are driven away” (15:34). Whoever follows Satan will share Hell as a full recompense: mawfūran denotes a recompense paid completely, with nothing withheld.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains that Satan’s “voice” is a metaphor for swiftly goading Adam’s descendants into disobedience through false whispers and ideas devoid of truth, like driving animals from behind with meaningless cries. His forces “riding and on foot” are likewise metaphorical: some assistants act quickly, like cavalry, while others operate more slowly, like infantry, but all drive people toward disobedience.

Satan’s sharing in wealth and children means sharing in the benefit people seek from them. He shares in wealth when it is unlawfully acquired, or when lawfully acquired wealth is spent in disobedience: the person obtains a worldly benefit while Satan gains the unlawfulness and the person is left without God’s mercy. He shares in children through unlawful begetting, or through raising and disciplining a legitimately born child in ways displeasing to God.

The commentary presents this as a general interpretation that encompasses reported applications. Ibn ʿAbbās and others identify Satan’s share with unlawfully acquired wealth and children born out of wedlock. Qatādah is reported to include making animals sāʾibah and baḥirah, and making children Jews, Christians, and Magians. Al-Kalbī is reported to have identified unlawful income and intercourse; other reports include naming children ʿAbd Shams or ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, burying daughters alive, and making offerings to false gods.

Satan’s promises are wholly ghurūr, intense deception: he displays error as rightness and falsehood as truth.
verses.65: Al-Mizan explains that Satan has no authority over God’s servants who do not deviate. God is sufficient as their wakīl: He watches over them and their actions, attends to their welfare, and governs their affairs. The verse therefore concerns God’s special guardianship of His non-deviating servants.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains that God speeds ships across the sea by the winds and other forces He sends and by making water fluid and navigable. Yuzjī, from izjāʾ, means moving or driving something from one state to another, and al-fulk is the plural of falkah, a ship.

Seeking of God’s grace means seeking sustenance and livelihood. Faḍl is bounty beyond what is needed, and min may indicate either the source of this grace or a part of it. The verse grounds these provisions in God’s enduring mercy and prepares for the verse that follows.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that distress in the sea is the danger of drowning amid violent waves and winds. Some exegetes take ḍalāl here to mean that the beings invoked are forgotten or lost from the mind. On that reading, duʿāʾ means requesting aid, so that all those normally invoked—including God—are forgotten except God, making the exception connected. Others take calling to mean worship, making the exception disconnected: the worshipped false gods are forgotten, while God is not.

The commentary prefers the usual sense of ḍalāl, losing one’s way, through a figurative image. When a person in peril thinks to seek help, the false gods formerly invoked seem to rush toward his heart but lose their way and fail to reach his memory. His attention thus turns to God, who is always witnessed by the heart though the person had turned away from Him; God answers and brings him safely to land. On this account, those called upon are the false gods, and the exception is disconnected, since imagery of rushing and following a path cannot be applied to God.

The sequel confirms that calling is requesting aid: outside distress, the polytheists neglect God and do not continuously call upon Him, whereas the present-tense tadʿūna denotes their habitual invocation of their false gods. Their turning aside after rescue means turning away from God or from calling upon Him. Yet turning aside itself presupposes an object present to one’s awareness; it thus hints that fiṭrah continually directs human beings toward God in hardship and ease alike.

Human ingratitude arises from attachment to apparent means, which makes people forget their real Cause and Creator despite His manifest and hidden blessings. Their neglect in ease is therefore not their original, natural condition and cannot disprove God’s Lordship; it is an evil habit of ingratitude. The verse proves God’s unity in Lordship: when all visible means fail, the heart still clings to a cause able to do what they cannot. This natural inclination entails a cause above all causes, to whom all affairs return—God—though worldly adornment, dependence on visible means, and heedlessness conceal Him.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains that yakhsifa means that the earth covers and swallows a person; khusūf is the covering of the moon’s disc in an eclipse. According to Majmaʿ al-bayān, a ḥāṣib is a wind carrying small stones and gravel, though it is also described as a destructive land-wind, in contrast with the sea-wind mentioned in the next verse.

The verse is a rebuking rhetorical question. Those who cease calling upon God after reaching land have no assurance against its dangers any more than against those of the sea. God may cause the land to swallow them or send a destructive tornado, and then they will find no protector to repel the affliction or restore their security.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that qaṣf is violent breaking and shattering, and qāṣif is a gale that breaks ships and buildings, or a deadly wind at sea. Fīhi refers to the sea. Tabīʿ, like tābiʿ, denotes one who follows; bihi may refer to the drowning, the sending of the wind, or both as events already done.

The verse completes the preceding rebuke: after rescue onto land, people cannot be secure that God will not return them to the sea, send a ship-breaking gale, and drown them for their ingratitude. No one will then pursue God over their drowning, demand an account from Him, or blame Him. The shift from the third person to the majestic plural in “against Us” displays divine grandeur and prepares for the following verses’ use of the majestic plural.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan reads “And surely We have honored the children of Adam” in a context of divine bounty and admonition. God carries human beings on land and sea, provides them with sustenance, and grants them security, yet they forget their Lord after deliverance from distress. The verse concerns all mankind, including polytheists, unbelievers, and sinners, rather than a special spiritual rank held only by some people.

Takrīm, honor, is an absolute bestowal of distinctive value and status, whereas tafḍīl, preferment, is a relative bestowal of more than others receive in matters shared between them. Humanity’s distinctive honor is ʿaql, the intellect by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, good from evil, and benefit from harm. From it flow such capacities as speech, writing, social organization, employing other creatures for human ends, and the immense development and variety of human life. By contrast, other natural beings possess only limited, fixed forms of planning and direction.

The various features mentioned by exegetes and reports—upright form, hands and fingers, eating with the hand, beauty, speech, writing, dominion over creatures, and the subjection of other things to human use—are particular illustrations. Some are consequences of intellect, and some illustrate relative preferment rather than honor. Other suggested examples, such as Adam’s creation by God’s hand and Muḥammad’s selection from mankind, are otherworldly or spiritual favors and lie outside this verse’s context. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the claim reported from Rūḥ al-maʿānī that all such examples equally constitute the honor intended here, just as it rejects restricting the honor to a single one of them.

God’s carrying of human beings refers to their conveyance by ships, animals, and similar means in pursuit of sustenance. His provision of good things includes pleasing and beneficial foods, fruits, crops, and every form of rizq. These are concrete instances after the general statement of honor: like honoring a guest by inviting him, sending him a mount, and then serving him good food.

The preferment over “many” creatures concerns humanity’s natural and material existence. The relevant creatures are animals and jinn, including intelligible species of animals that the Qur’an treats as communities; it does not concern angels, who are transcendent and not subject to the material system. Thus humanity is honored by the uniquely bestowed intellect and preferred relatively in shared natural matters: food, drink, clothing, dwelling, mating, family organization, and social institutions. Human beings develop these in diverse and continually advancing forms beyond the simple forms found among animals.

Al-Mizan rejects explanations reported from Majmaʿ al-bayān that equate takrīm and tafḍīl, divide them into worldly and otherworldly blessings, or make the former the basis for responsibility and the latter the imposed duties that raise people to high stations. The claim that tafḍīl necessarily adds an unmerited favor is also unfounded, since preferment may occur where its recipient deserves it. Likewise, it rejects Rāzī’s assignment of intrinsic endowments to takrīm and acquired perfections to tafḍīl. Both are indeed divine favors, but that division does not accord with the terms’ lexical or ordinary usage; the proper distinction remains absolute honor versus relative preferment.

Accordingly, the verse is silent about whether humans or angels are superior in spiritual merit. The interpretation of kathīr as “all,” and min as merely explanatory, is implausible, unsupported, and contrary to the context. Nor can “many” be made to mean “all” by analogies in which an adjective describes an undivided whole. Even if the verse were merely silent about angels, that would not prove their superiority, nor would a generic superiority of angels preclude individual humans, such as prophets, from surpassing them. The correct point is that human beings are superior to animals and jinn in their physical existence, while angels are outside the comparison.

Al-Mizan then considers the dispute over human and angelic superiority. Ashʿarites commonly maintain that believing humans are superior, sometimes appealing to this verse by treating “many” as “all” and to reports that the believer is more honored than angels. Many Shias likewise argue that a believer’s obedience is greater because he can obey or disobey, whereas angels are created obedient and lack the drives of appetite, anger, and desire. Yet this is not unanimous among Ashʿarites: al-Zajjāj, and a view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, make angels absolutely superior; other rankings place human messengers first, then angel messengers, then other angels and humans; and Rāzī, attributing the view to al-Ghazzālī, places the Cherub angels first, followed by human messengers, perfect humans, and the remaining angels above ordinary humans. Muʿtazilites argue for angelic superiority from the apparent wording of the verse. Al-Zamakhsharī sharply rejects reading “many” as “all,” holding that the creatures intended are other than angels and that proximity to angels is itself enough honor for humanity.

A reported account, transmitted from the Prophet through Ibn ʿUmar, Anas b. Mālik, Zayd b. Aslam, and Jābir b. ʿAbd-Allāh al-Anṣārī, has angels ask that the hereafter be assigned to them because humans have worldly eating, drinking, mating, and riding; God is reported to answer that He will not equate Adam’s descendants, created by His hands, with those created by “Be.” Al-Mizan finds the content untenable: bodily activities preserve material human existence and yield pleasures connected with that need, while angels already possess the perfection humans seek through these burdensome acts and are not subject to the material order or deprived of such things.

The same problem affects the claim that voluntary human obedience necessarily exceeds angelic obedience. In human social judgment, obedience earns greater reward when a person can equally obey or disobey, and is more difficult where temptation is greater. But if the angels’ inability to sin stripped their obedience of merit, their acts could only metaphorically be called obedience, and their nearness to God would lack any ground in their own worth. This conflicts with God’s praise of them as honored servants who do not precede Him in speech and act only by His command (21:26-27), who do not disobey Him (66:6), and who worship, fear, glorify, and serve Him without weariness.

The capacity to act or refrain is not itself the criterion of virtue; it has moral value only insofar as it reveals good will and pure intention. The obedience of a hypocrite or one whose heart is diseased has no worth despite outward effort. Virtue lies in purity of soul, soundness of essence, and sincerity in servitude, which may appear in obedience, abstention from sin, and endurance of hardship. Angels, whose essence is pure and noble and whose acts are wholly humble, sincere service of God, therefore surpass humans in constitution and in the purity of their acts. Human acts are rarely free from concealed polytheism, egoism, and carnal inclination; the perfection humans pursue by obedience is given to angels from their creation.

Nevertheless, because human beings gradually actualize their essential potentials, they may attain a degree of nearness and perfection higher than that which angels possess by their original nature. The Qur’an apparently confirms this possibility in humanity’s capacity to know all the names, a perfection the angels could not gain merely through praise and sanctification, and in their prostration to Adam. That prostration signified humility before the station of human perfection: Adam was their qiblah and a symbol of humanity. The commentary says this apparent Qur’anic teaching is also supported by narrations.

For verse (17:71), Al-Mizan explains that the omitted command is “Remember” the Day of Resurrection. An Imam is a leader who is followed. The Qur’an applies the title both to those who guide by God’s command and to leaders of unbelief and misguidance. Although it can also call the Torah an Imam and apparently applies the term to the Guarded Tablet, neither meaning fits here: every people has its own Imam, whereas the Guarded Tablet is one and belongs to no people in particular; and the verse applies to every people, including those before Noah’s scripture and divine law.

The Imam of each people therefore means the person they actually followed on the path of truth or falsehood. Restricting it to a God-appointed true leader is unlikely, because Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and misguided people are not separated from their false leaders. The unqualified wording “their Imam,” together with the sequel, points to the leader people adopted and followed in worldly life, whether true or false, not merely a rightful leader whom they may have abandoned.

Calling people by their Imam does not mean calling them by labels such as the nation of Abraham or the people of Pharaoh. It means gathering and summoning them with their leaders. Those who followed a true leader receive their books in their right hands; those who failed to recognize and follow their true Imam manifest their blindness. This connection establishes two kinds of Imam: leaders of guidance and leaders of misguidance.

Al-Mizan rejects interpreting Imam as the scriptures people followed, as the record of deeds, as the Guarded Tablet, or as each nation’s collective record. A book of deeds reports actions and follows them; it is not a leader, and it does not issue God’s final judgment. These readings also fail to fit the individual receiving his own book. It likewise rejects the rare proposal that Imam is the plural of umm, so that people are called by their mothers: the wording requires every people to be called by its Imam, not every individual by his mother, and even an authenticated report to that effect would be independent of this verse. Al-Kashshāf calls that interpretation an innovation.

The broader proposal that Imam includes every followed person, religion, scripture, custom, or false doctrine is also unnecessary. In Qur’anic usage, an Imam is a leader of divine guidance or misguidance; the guidance of books and religions ultimately derives from their leaders, and their misguidance from their founders and innovators. The bāʾ in bi-imāmihim may denote accompaniment or instrumentality.

Receiving one’s book in the right hand follows from being gathered with one’s Imam. Fatīl is the fine thread in a date stone’s split. The rightly guided group reads its record with joy as felicitous people and receives its reward fully, without injustice even to the measure of a date-thread.

verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” means this world, in contrast with the hereafter. The blindness in both realms is blindness of inner perception, baṣīrah, not bodily sight, as is confirmed by “and more erring from the way.” Those who fail in this world to recognize the true Imam and follow the true path will not attain salvation, felicity, forgiveness, or mercy in the hereafter.

The commentary therefore rejects the view that blindness in this world means failure to recognize and thank God’s preceding blessings. It also rejects the view that worldly blindness is inner blindness while blindness in the hereafter is merely physical, since physical blindness there ultimately reduces to lack of insight when hidden things are made manifest. One exegete’s wording may take the second aʿmā as comparative—more intensely blind—and the context supports this.
verses.73: Al-Mizan explains that wa in here means “surely,” while fitnah is making someone slip or turn away, and khalīl means a friend, deriving from al-khullah rather than, improbably, al-khallah, “need.” What God revealed is the Qur’an as containing monotheism, the repudiation of partners for God, and righteous instruction. This accords with reports that the polytheists asked the Prophet to cease condemning their gods, dismiss their believing slaves, and separate himself from lower-class Muslims so that they might sit and hear him. The verse means that they nearly sought to turn him from the revealed course, so that his contrary action would amount to forging against God what He had not revealed; only then would they have taken him as a friend.
verses.74: Al-Mizan takes God’s “establishment” (tathbīt) to mean His protection and prevention. Rukūn means inclination, or even the slightest inclination. By saying that the Prophet would have been near to inclining, rather than that he inclined, and by speaking of inclination toward them rather than merely toward their request, the verse negates every degree of concession. God’s protection meant that he neither accepted their demand, nor inclined to them at all, nor even came near to such inclination.
verses.75: Al-Mizan reads the verse as a threat: had the Prophet even come near to a slight inclination toward them, God would have made him taste twice the punishment inflicted on evildoers in this life and twice that inflicted after death. The final clause intensifies the warning: under such punishment he would find no helper against God and no escape. Majmaʿ al-bayān narrates from Abān b. Taghlib that ḍiʿf means punishment twice as painful as ordinary punishment, supported by poetic usage in which ḍiʿf denotes intense pain or punishment.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains istifzāz as driving or moving something lightly and easily, and khilāfa as “afterwards.” “The land” denotes the known land of Mecca. Thus, the polytheists were close to expelling the Prophet from Mecca; had they done so, they would have remained after him only a short time before perishing. The view that the verse concerns Jews seeking to expel him from Medina, or both Jews and polytheists expelling him from Arabia, is unlikely: the sūrah is Meccan and contextually unified, whereas the Prophet’s conflict with the Jews occurred after the migration.

Verse (17:77) continues the preceding warning. Sunnah, with an implied phrase, means God’s established course with His earlier messengers: He destroys the polytheists who expel their messengers from their towns. This course is attributed to the messengers because it was instituted for their sake, and taḥwīl denotes moving something from one state to another. Accordingly, if they had expelled the Prophet, God would certainly have destroyed them, for His course admits no alteration or replacement.

verses.78:
Al-Mizan notes that dulūk means the sun’s decline; al-Mubarrid extends dulūk al-shams from its noon descent to sunset. Ghasaq al-layl is the onset, or intense darkness, of night. Although exegetes differ over the verse’s first clause, Shiʿa narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt interpret dulūk al-shams as noon and ghasaq al-layl as midnight. On this interpretation, the span from noon to midnight includes the obligatory Noon, Afternoon, Sunset, and Evening Prayers, while “the morning recitation” adds the Morning Prayer; thus the verse encompasses all five daily prayers.

“The morning recitation” means the Morning Prayer, so called because it includes Qur’anic recitation, and the narrations unanimously interpret it this way. Shiʿa and Sunni narrations also agree that it is “witnessed” by both the angels of night and the angels of day.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains tahajjud as rising after sleep. In “pray tahajjud for it,” bihi refers to the Qur’an in the preceding verse, though it may refer to part of the night; the command is to keep vigil after sleep in prayer with the Qur’an. Nāfilatan laka means that this prayer is additional to the obligatory prayers.

The “praised station” may grammatically mean either a raising of great glory or a station bestowed while the Prophet is raised. Because God describes it absolutely as maḥmūd, it must be a station praised by everyone, one from which all are pleased and benefit. The exegetes therefore identify it with the Prophet’s greatest intercession (al-shafāʿat al-kubrā) on the Day of Resurrection, an interpretation confirmed by Sunni and Shiʿa narrations from the Prophet and the Imams.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains mudkhal and mukhraj as entering and exiting. Their being “of truth” means that every entering and leaving is genuine and accords with truth: outward and inward do not differ, its parts do not conflict, and speech, action, and belief correspond. The Prophet must not call people to God outwardly while inwardly seeking authority, nor pursue mixed aims in different parts of his call. This is the station of the most truthful (al-ṣiddīqīn).

The requested power from God is assistance and dominance in all that he undertakes, so that no false argument defeats his call (daʿwah), no trouble or enemy plot ensnares him, and no satanic whisper or incitement misleads him. The verse is absolute, asking God to govern all his affairs according to truth and give him authority by which he neither departs from truth nor manifests falsehood. Therefore it provides no evidence for restricting the entering and exiting to migration to Medina and the conquest of Mecca, or to death and resurrection. In light of its sequence, it includes seeking God’s refuge in every matter of his call, including every place where he settles, enters, or leaves.
verses.81: Al-Mizan reports that Majmaʿ al-bayān defines zuhūq as destruction and annulment; zahaqat nafsuhu is said when a soul departs toward death and destruction. The verse commands the Prophet to proclaim the advent of truth and the disappearance of falsehood. In the context of the polytheists’ efforts to turn him away, it tells them to despair of influencing him. It also establishes that falsehood has no endurance or stability, as expressed in: And the parable of an evil word is as an evil tree pulled up from the earth's surface; it has no stability (14:26).
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that min in “of the Qur’an” is descriptive: what is revealed as healing and mercy is the Qur’an itself. Calling it shifāʾ presupposes that hearts, like bodies, have health and disease. Human beings are created with an innate disposition toward true beliefs about origin and end, their implications, and the virtues and conduct harmonious with them. Spiritual disorder is therefore a disease, while the Qur’an is its remedy.

Disease of heart is not simply unbelief or hypocrisy. It includes doubts and suspicions that unsettle the soul, incline it toward falsehood and desire, and may remain alongside the lowest degree of faith, though they are imperfection and a kind of polytheism compared with higher faith. By decisive proofs and illuminating arguments, the Qur’an removes doubts that obstruct true belief; by its admonitions, stories, parables, promises, warnings, glad tidings, laws, and prescriptions, it cures defects of heart.

Mercy, by contrast, is a gift that completes an imperfection and meets a need. Having removed ignorance, blindness, doubt, agitation, and base traits, the Qur’an gives hearts knowledge, certainty, noble spiritual states, and moral virtues. Thus, as healing it clears the impediments to felicity and prepares the heart for salvation; as mercy it restores the innate soundness it lacked and clothes it in felicity and fortitude. Mercy follows healing because restoration follows the removal of illness.

The commentary holds that “the unjust” means all unbelievers, not merely polytheists. Their designation as unjust explains why the Qur’an increases their khasāran: they began with the capital of innate religion in their uncorrupted souls, but disbelief in God and His signs diminished it. Their disbelief in and wrongful turning from the Qur’an is then an additional loss, which is why the verse says that it adds to them only perdition.

A proposed interpretation includes physical as well as spiritual healing through seeking blessing from the Qur’an in recitation and writing. Al-Mizan finds no objection to this, provided the latter half is treated consistently: as such use protects believers from pain and illness, it also protects them from the injustice and schemes of unbelievers, thereby adding to the latter’s loss. The Qur’an’s addition of perdition is metaphorical, however; their own wrongdoing and voluntary evil choice truly cause it.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains that aʿraḍa, to turn aside, and naʾā bi-jānibihi, to distance oneself by one’s side, portray a person’s cutting himself off from his Lord when favor is bestowed; the latter expression can also denote pride and vainglory. When even a slight evil touches him, he despairs of the good, namely favor. The verse attributes favor to God but does not attribute evil to Him, clearing Him of direct ascription of evil.

Evil is relative rather than absolute: death, disease, poverty, and loss are evil for the afflicted person, but can be good and unavoidable within the universal order. What is intended primarily and in itself is good and is directly decreed by God; evil is intended accidentally, for the sake of something else. The verse describes the ordinary person shaped by social habits: when apparent means yield wealth, power, children, and other blessings, he attaches himself to those means, forgets God, and fails to remember and thank Him. When these means are lost, he sees no other source of good and despairs.

This is not the state of one who preserves fiṭrah, whether through special divine aid or through an emergency that makes apparent means vanish from view and returns him to his Lord. Humanity may be in its innate state, which turns to God in distress, or its habituated state, in which means veil it from Him. The verse concerns the latter and therefore does not conflict with verses saying that people call upon God in affliction. It also explains why the unjust are near to perdition: favors make them turn proudly away, while adversity makes them despair.

In the philosophical discussion, Al-Mizan reports the view of some Muslim scholars that evils fall under divine decree accidentally (bil-ʿaraḍ). A report from Plato illustrates the claim that evil is non-existential: in a killing, the killer’s power and courage, the sword’s sharpness, and the victim’s susceptibility to being cut are each perfections; the evil is the loss of the victim’s life. Yet evils occur with real events and thus are not absolutely, but relatively, non-existential. Loss, deficiency, death, and corruption are subject to the universal divine order only through the existential events with which they accompany, not essentially in themselves.

Two kinds of nonexistence must be distinguished. Absolute nonexistence, considered by itself, is merely mental and is no evil; relative lacks belonging to quiddities—such as a plant’s not being an animal—are necessary conceptual consequences of their determinations, not created realities. The relevant kind is privation: the absence of a perfection in a subject capable of it, such as blindness in one capable of sight. Defects, disease, pain, and corruption are privations found only in material subjects and arise from the recipient’s limited capacity, not from the Donor of Existence. A non-existential effect has a non-existential cause.

What God essentially wills and decrees in each thing is its existent aspect, according to its receptivity; the deficiency accompanying it belongs to that receptivity. Deficiency may be called created or bestowed only accidentally because it is united with the existent aspect. Of possible things, only the purely good and that whose good exceeds its evil are brought into being. Things of equal good and evil, predominant evil, or pure evil would entail preferring without a determinant or preferring the inferior. Divine wisdom, inseparable from infinite power, knowledge, and generosity, therefore creates the best system; the little evil found exists for and through the greater good.

Imam al-Rāzī objects that philosophers make God a complete cause inseparable from His effect, rendering His action compulsory rather than chosen. Al-Mizan replies that necessity belongs to the effect as received from its cause, not to the cause; an effect cannot turn back to compel its cause. The author of Rūḥ al-maʿānī, as reported, likewise says that God’s will is not indifferent between an event and its opposite without wisdom. Philosophers who affirm divine choice do not liken God’s action to fire’s necessary burning; even if they did, they would still need to explain evil, lest pure good as Creator imply the dualist doctrine of separate causes for good and evil.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains shākilah as the manner, character, makeup, or path that confines a person to what it demands. Whether it is understood as character or as a path, the verse means that action conforms to the actor’s shākilah. Actions and bodily movements disclose the immaterial form of the spirit: the brave and timid, generous and stingy, act differently. Psychological traits also have affinities with bodily temperaments, some tending toward anger, vengeance, or quick excitation of desire.

Such bodily dispositions are only propensity and tendency (iqtiḍāʾ), not complete causation. They do not abolish free choice or make contrary action impossible, however difficult it may be. The universality of the religious call and the fact that religion belongs to the unchanging fiṭrah show that physical makeup cannot compel a person to depart from the balance to which his innate nature calls him.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that salvation and damnation are inseparable essential properties of persons, or are fixed by an unavoidable eternal decree such that religious calls merely complete an argument. If felicity and wretchedness belonged necessarily to essences, proof and argument would be pointless, since proofs do not apply to essential properties. If they were imposed by an eternal decree, people rather than God would have the argument against God. Human life itself—education, training, warnings, promises, threats, commands, and prohibitions—shows that a person stands between the paths of salvation and damnation and can choose either; recompense corresponds to striving.

External conditions also shape character. Inherited norms, customs, habits, and the surrounding social environment establish patterns in the soul and urge conformity. These, too, operate by tendency rather than necessity, though acquired vice or virtue may become so entrenched that reform no longer has hope. This does not invalidate religious proof against those whose hearts have been sealed, because the ineffectualness of the call results from their own evil choice; a chosen impossibility does not negate choice.

A person has two interwoven shākilahs: an initial character arising from created bodily composition and temperament (mizāj), and a second character formed by the impressions of external circumstances. Once qualities have become actualized, every action—speech and silence, movement and rest—reflects the inner character. The visible is a sign of the hidden, just as an action represents its actor.

In the present context, the second sense of shākilah is more probable: character as the combined outcome of physical makeup and external influences. The verse answers why the Qur’an heals and mercies believers but increases the unjust in loss. Those with a just character readily receive right speech and righteous action and benefit from the call of truth; those with an unjust character find them difficult and the call adds to their perdition. God best knows the inward character and who is best guided. Yet unjust character does not necessitate misguidance; it retains a weak trace of guidance, while the just character is ahdā, more rightly guided. The unjust can still cease their injustice and benefit from the Qur’an.

Al-Mizan records Imam al-Rāzī’s view that differing responses to the Qur’an prove that souls differ in quiddity: pure souls receive further light, while impure souls receive further loss, as the same sun has differing effects on different things. The commentary grants that such an argument could concern souls after firmly rooted traits and formations have developed, but not souls in their initial simple state before acquired second natures. The verse concerns formed personal character, which inclines rather than compels action.

In its philosophical discussion, Al-Mizan presents the philosophers’ doctrine of an essential existential congruence between action and actor, effect and efficient cause (al-ʿillat al-fāʿiliyyah). The effect is a lower degree of its cause’s existence, for without a real tie, no particular action could truly be attributed to a particular actor. As the giver cannot lack what it gives, the efficient cause possesses the effect’s existential perfection at a higher degree.

Mullā Ṣadrā, as reported, makes this dependence more precise: an effect’s need and attachment to its cause cannot be subsequent to its essence, or it would be independent in itself and thus not an effect. Its very existence is relation (rābiṭ) to the cause; its apparent independence is really the independence of its cause reflected on a lower plane.

From the Qur’anic standpoint, all things and every aspect of their existence are āyahs of God, reflecting His names and attributes as a mirror reflects what stands before it. Nothing can be independent in any respect, for then it would not be a sign in that respect. Created things are therefore God’s acts, and their existence and attributes indicate His existence and attributes. This is the proper meaning of the congruence of action and actor, not that an act literally possesses the existence or essence of its actor.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that rūḥ may lexically denote the source of animal life, sensation, and voluntary motion, and may figuratively denote what gives souls life, such as knowledge, revelation, or guidance. But the Qur’anic uses of al-rūḥ show that it cannot always mean the animal soul. In passages where the spirit stands with or descends alongside the angels, it is distinct from them; a hadith attributed to ʿAlī likewise uses (16:2) to establish that rūḥ is not identical with the angels. Its descriptions as holy and faithful indicate purity from the disloyalty and defilements found in human souls.

The spirit accompanies angels in the descent of revelation. Although revelation of the Qur’an to the Prophet’s heart is attributed in one place to Gabriel, it is elsewhere attributed to the Faithful Spirit and the Holy Spirit. Al-Mizan concludes that Gabriel descends with the spirit, while the spirit carries the recited Qur’an. Accordingly, “And thus did We reveal to you a spirit (rūḥan) of Our command (42:52)” means the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Prophet accompanied by the Qur’an; it does not mean that the Qur’an itself is called spirit. Though revelation is covert communication and the spirit an external real being, the latter may be called revelation because sacred creatures are God’s words, that is, signs indicating His intended meaning. Jesus too is called God’s Word and a spirit because he was directly created by the divine word “Be!” without ordinary means.

In “The spirit is of the command of my Lord,” min indicates genus: the spirit is of the nature of divine command, as in similar verses concerning the spirit and command. God’s command is His address “Be!”—the existentiating word (kalimat al-ījād), which is His act of creation considered as directly related and dependent upon Him. It is one and non-gradual, beyond time, space, and physical means. Material things have two aspects: their gradual, mediated aspect, called creation (khalq), and their non-gradual direct relation to God, called command (amr), word, and speech. Adam’s creation from dust and then the divine “Be!” illustrate these two aspects; the reference to a human embryo becoming “another creation” also indicates an aspect not involving physical means.

The command of every thing is its malakūt, its transcendent divine aspect. Thus the spirit has the mode of existence of the divine command and belongs to the malakūt of things, transcending nature and time. The Qur’an speaks of the spirit as a separate entity beside angels; as accompanying them in revelation; as breathed into humanity; as strengthening believers; and as sent upon prophets. The life of animals and plants may also allude to spirit, since life apparently proceeds from it.

The question in (17:85) therefore concerns the reality of rūḥ in its general Qur’anic applications, and the reply positively explains it as belonging to the divine command. “You are not given aught of knowledge but a little” means that the knowledge granted about its exalted station, remarkable properties, and cosmic effects is only a small portion.

The commentary rejects several interpretations. Restricting the question to the spirit that stands with angels in certain verses has no stated proof. Equating it with Gabriel fails because a word’s use for Gabriel in one passage does not govern every occurrence; otherwise Gabriel and Jesus, both called spirit, would be identical. Equating it with the Qur’an wrongly assumes that 42:52 calls the Qur’an spirit and is not required by the following verse. Taking it as merely the human spirit is not the primary Qur’anic sense, and the materialist descriptions proposed for it are refuted by the preceding analysis. The view that the verse asks whether rūḥ is originated (muḥdath, ḥādith) or pre-eternal (qadīm) is correct only insofar as it concerns rūḥ generally; the wording gives no evidence that origination and pre-eternity are the question.

Whether the reply is a positive explanation or a refusal to answer depends on these differing interpretations; Al-Mizan takes it as explanatory. The address, “You are not given aught of knowledge but a little,” apparently continues the Prophet’s answer to the questioners. It is most likely addressed to the Jews, who were known for religious knowledge and to whom the verse implicitly grants some knowledge, rather than to Quraysh or pagan Arabs, elsewhere described as having no knowledge.
verses.86:
Al-Mizan connects this verse with the preceding discussion of the spirit. Although that discussion concerned spirit generally, its foremost application here is the celestial spirit that descends upon the Prophet and inspires the Qur’an. The verse apparently means—and God knows best—that this spirit belongs to God’s command and lies wholly within His power: if He willed, He would take away the spirit, His word cast upon the Prophet, and no one could protect the Prophet against God or compel the return of what was taken.

Thus “that which We have revealed to you” refers to the divine spirit inspired to the Prophet, as in “And thus did We reveal to you a spirit (rūḥan) of our command (42:52),” rather than simply to the Qur’an considered apart from the descending spirit. Wakīl means one who could rise on the Prophet’s behalf to demand back what God removed, not one who would help him preserve or recite the Qur’an. The latter interpretation follows only if the revealed thing is taken to mean the Qur’an itself.
verses.87: Al-Mizan explains the exception as qualifying an implied statement: the Prophet was given and chosen for the descent and companionship of the spirit solely through mercy from his Lord. “Surely His grace to you is abundant” states the abundant divine favor that accounts for this mercy.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains that ẓahīr means helper or assistant, and that the repeated phrase “the like of” simply refers both times to the Qur’an. The verse is an explicit taḥaddī: even if all human beings and jinn joined in mutual assistance, they could not produce its like.

The challenge concerns all the Qur’an’s perfections of language and meaning, not eloquence and rhetoric alone; otherwise it would not extend to non-Arabs, although the verse includes all men and jinn. It also remains ongoing: the masters of Arabic eloquence are gone, yet the Qur’an endures as a miracle and continues to challenge all to bring its like.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains taṣrīf of similitudes as presenting and repeating them in diverse formulations, while a mathal illustrates an intended meaning and brings it near to the hearer’s mind. Min in “of every kind of similitude” identifies what has been repeatedly explained; it does not mean only some similitudes. The Qur’an has therefore presented every kind of explanatory likeness that clarifies the path of truth and calls people to faith and gratitude.

The verse rebukes most people for refusing anything but kufūr—both denial and ingratitude. Its explicit repetition of al-nās, rather than using a pronoun, perhaps indicates that this ingratitude results from their human condition. Despite the Qur’an’s recurrent explanations calling them to belief and thankfulness for divine blessings, most persist in denial and ingratitude.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains that Quraysh made belief conditional upon the Prophet’s producing a perpetual spring from Mecca’s dry land; possessing a garden of palms and grapes with gushing rivers; bringing down a piece of heaven; bringing God and the angels visibly before them; possessing a house of gold; or ascending to heaven and bringing down a readable book. These demands derogate the Qur’an, the enduring miracle. Yanbūʿ is an unfailing spring; tafjīr is an intensive splitting or gushing forth; khilāl means among or in the midst; kisaf means pieces; qabīlan means face to face; zukhruf is gold; and ruqiyy is ascent.

Their language attributes each act directly to the Prophet: they do not ask him to request it from his Lord. Most demands require divine supernatural power, and some—such as bringing God and the angels face to face—are essentially impossible. Their demand thus assumes that he is responsible for exercising unlimited divine power.

His reply begins, “Glory be to my Lord,” both to declare God free from delegating His absolute power to him and, fittingly, to express amazement at their request. “Am I aught but a mortal messenger?” refutes their expectation in two ways. As a mortal, he cannot perform such acts from his own power. As a messenger, his office is to receive and convey God’s command, warnings, and glad tidings; it does not confer delegated authority to create whatever he wishes. The Prophet never claimed such a station.

Al-Mizan rejects an exegete’s view that “mortal” was added merely to rebut a supposed denial that mortals can be messengers, while “messenger” alone supplies the argument. Nothing in these verses mentions such a denial. That reading also makes likeness to prior messengers the unstated main argument, disrupting the flow. Further, reports claiming that the polytheists asked the Prophet only to ask God for these signs cannot override the Qur’an’s explicit wording, which attributes the demanded acts to him directly. Nor is any reason provided for the assertion that “mortal” and “messenger” cannot stand as two predicates.

verses.94: Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question, “What! has Allah raised up a mortal to be a messenger?” conveys denial, whether or not it reproduces their exact spoken words. “People” means the polytheists, and believing means believing in God’s messengers. What kept Quraysh and most Arabs from accepting the Prophet’s messengership was their denial that a human being could be a divine messenger. This was their recurring response to messengers: had God willed, they claimed, He would have sent angels rather than human envoys.
verses.95:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as a refutation of the claim that humans cannot be messengers or receive revelation. God’s gracious will to guide the inhabitants of earth requires a guidance descending from heaven, not one generated by themselves. Earthly life is material life, and its guidance requires an angelic messenger descending with revelation. Even if angels themselves lived materially on earth as settled walkers, God would send down an angel messenger to them as well.

The verse’s central premises are therefore that life on earth is material and that divine grace guides such life through revelation brought by an angel. The common explanation—that the messenger must merely belong to the same species as those addressed—is not the fundamental point, though a human messenger does educate people from among them. Material life entails differing degrees of purity, perfection, felicity, and wretchedness. Although angels descend with revelation for humanity generally, only a human being purified from material defilement and untouched by devils can receive it directly. Such persons are the human messengers.

This rests on a broader proof of prophethood. Every species needs divine guidance toward perfection and felicity. Human happiness requires social laws and customs that secure welfare in this world and the next and resolve inevitable disputes. Human reason alone cannot furnish these, since it is itself a source of disagreement. Humanity therefore needs another faculty of perception, shuʿūr or waḥy, through which it receives divine teaching and law; the human who possesses it is a prophet. The present verse adds that this revelation must descend through an angel from heaven.

A human messenger is thus one to whom an angel descends with God’s religion and who conveys it by God’s command. Earthly life and God’s care for human perfection necessitate the descent of religion through angels; the individual who sees the angel and receives its message must possess inner purity and a spirit of divine command. The angel’s descent is a universal grace for humanity, even though direct reception has particular recipients.

The wording “We would certainly have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger,” rather than simply raising an angel among them, decisively confronts the idolaters’ misconception. Al-Mizan says that idolaters could accept perfect earthly reformers, or even divine descent and embodied beings, while worshipping angels, jinn, or deified humans; what they rejected was an angel sent from God with a religion commanding worship of God alone. The wording also shows that the angel is sent to all humans, while only one fit human receives it directly.

The meaning of risālah inferred here confirms narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt: a rasūl sees the angel of revelation and hears its voice, whereas a nabī sees dreams but does not see the angel while awake. Finally, “angels walking about as settlers” subtly identifies earthly material life, for bodily walking on earth under gravity is a distinctive feature of it.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that, after the Qur’an’s challenge and the arguments for the Prophet’s messengership, the polytheists continued in defiance, denial, disrespect for truth, and demands for baseless signs. The Prophet is therefore commanded to leave the matter to God’s witness. He conveyed his message, called them, argued with them, and left no excuse; they heard it and God’s proof was completed against them, yet they rebelled. The verse declares the end of debate and defers judgment to the true Holder of command, who knows and sees His servants.

The proposed interpretation that God’s witness here primarily attests the truth of the call and the authenticity of the Prophet’s messengership is true in itself, especially through the inimitability of the Book. But it does not fit the wording “between me and you” or the conclusion that God is Aware of and Seeing His servants. Were that the intended point, the verse would instead speak of a witness for the Prophet against them or over his messengership.
verses.97:
Al-Mizan takes the statement on guidance as a continuation of the command to say that God suffices as witness. The proof against the polytheists has been completed, their misguidance has become due, and there is no further hope of their guidance. The Prophet is told to end the argument: guidance belongs to God alone, and one whom He does not guide has no guardian besides Him who can guide him. He should not burden himself with continuing to summon them in hope that they will believe.

The plural awliyāʾ is used because any supposed guardians besides God would be their many gods or their many material means. The shift from the majestic plural to the singular “Allah guides” may prevent any suggestion that angels share in guidance or misguidance, since the polytheists regarded angels as guardians and worshipped them.

The verse then states their requital: on the Day of Resurrection they will be gathered on their faces blind, dumb, and deaf; their dwelling is hell, whose burning is renewed whenever its flames subside. This punishment is for their disbelief in God’s communications and their denial that they could be resurrected after becoming bones and decayed particles.
