verses.99:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse argues for resurrection against those who deem it impossible once their bodies have become bones and decayed particles. The God who created the heavens and earth, and created their bodies in the first place, can create bodies like them again. The likeness concerns the newly created body compared with the former body, not the person’s identity. Identity and individuation belong to the soul, which is preserved with God and does not perish when the body disintegrates. When the same soul is attached to a new body, the resurrected person is exactly the worldly person, just as personal identity persists in this life despite continual bodily change.

The claim that the soul is fully retained is supported by the response that the Angel of Death takes people in full when they are “lost in the earth.” What is lost is only the body; the person himself is not lost and can receive a recreated body. The Qur’anic teachings of return to God, resurrection, questioning, reckoning, and requital likewise require that the resurrected human be the same person, not merely a similar one. Al-Mizan therefore questions the suggestion that “their like” simply means “the same.”

The appointed ajal apparently means death—either the full worldly lifespan bounded by it or its final end—not the Day of Resurrection. Its certainty is a reminder to take warning, cease defying God and denying His signs, and recognize that He can resurrect and requite them. Taking ajal as the Day of Resurrection does not fit a context that is already arguing for resurrection, nor does the phrase provide a clear independent proof of it. Their kufūr here means juḥūd, denial and rejection.
verses.100: Al-Mizan explains qatūr as one who withholds and restricts spending to an extreme degree. The verse censures those whose niggardliness would make them withhold even the treasures of their Lord’s mercy out of fear of expenditure. It addresses the disposition underlying their refusal to believe that God could raise a human messenger.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan holds that the nine clear signs given to Moses in his mission to Pharaoh were apparently the cane, the hand, the flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, droughts, and diminution of fruits. This accords with Moses’ statement that the Lord of the heavens and earth alone sent them as clear proof (17:102), and excludes such other miracles as the splitting of the sea and rock, reviving the slain man through the cow, reviving those struck by the quake, and raising the mountain over the Israelites.

Their gradual appearance is no objection, since the verse gives an overview of Moses’ whole conflict with Pharaoh; Al-Mizan therefore rejects alternative identifications of the nine signs. The Torah’s list differs, and perhaps for this reason the verse does not specify the signs but directs the Prophet to ask the Children of Israel; otherwise the Jews would have rejected a Book that contradicted their own.

Pharaoh’s description of Moses as masḥūran means that Moses had been bewitched and thereby lost his mind, like Pharaoh’s other Qur’anic accusation that the messenger was mad (26:27). Some have instead taken masḥūr to mean sāḥir, a sorcerer, but the verse’s meaning is clear.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses tells Pharaoh that he knows the clear signs came only from the Lord of the heavens and earth, as proofs by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. Moses then declares that Pharaoh will be mathbūran—destroyed or lost—because of his denial and defiance.

The use of ẓann in Moses’ statement may reflect that a person’s perdition is for God to decide; may answer Pharaoh’s own “I deem you” in (17:101); or may use ẓann in the sense of certainty (yaqīn).
verses.103: Al-Mizan explains istifzāz as driving people away by force: Pharaoh sought forcibly to expel them from the land, but God drowned him and all who were with him.
verses.104:
Al-Mizan identifies the land in which the Israelites were told to dwell as the holy land prescribed for them, while the “earth” from which Pharaoh sought to expel them may mean the earth generally or, contextually, Egypt. Lafifan means gathered together and intertwined.

The usual exegetical reading takes waʿd al-ākhirah as the second life, the Day of Resurrection: after Pharaoh’s drowning, the Israelites were commanded to settle in the holy land and would later be gathered for judgment and the settlement of disputes.

Al-Mizan considers it quite likely, however, that waʿd al-ākhirah instead refers to the earlier “second promise”: “So when the second promise (waʿd al-ākhirah) came that they may bring you to grief and that they may enter the mosque as they entered it the first time, and that they might destroy whatever they gained ascendancy over with utter destruction (17:7).” The verse would then conclude the chapter’s earlier discussion: Israel was to remain in the holy land until that promise, when killing, captivity, and exile would intertwine them, referring to their Babylonian captivity and exile. The consequential fāʾ in fa-idhā supports this latter reading, but not the Resurrection reading.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains that the Qur’an was revealed and came with truth, and is therefore secure from falsehood on God’s side: it is neither futile speech nor subject to future corruption or abrogation by co-authors. The Prophet’s role is only to give good news and warning through it.

Consequently, neither the Prophet nor anyone else may add to or omit from the Book, abandon any of it at popular request or personal desire, seek a substitute sign, compromise over it, or exempt people from its teachings and laws. As the word of truth from the source of truth, it admits no such manipulation: “And what is there after the truth but error?” (10:32). Thus the Qur’an itself is the true sign.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan connects this verse to the preceding one: the Qur’an was revealed with truth and revealed as a recitation in portions. Majmaʿ al-bayān explains faraqnāhu as faṣṣalnāhu: it was differentiated and sent down verse by verse and chapter by chapter, while mukth and makth mean pausing or tarrying.

Taken by itself, the verse indicates that Qur’anic teachings, whose original transcendent form is with God, descend as words and phrases gradually because people can receive, understand, and absorb them only piece by piece. The gradual division of beliefs and practical rulings enables knowledge to accompany practice and prevents people from being overwhelmed by the entire Book at once.

Yet the context makes a more specific sense more appropriate: the verse answers the demand that the Qur’an be sent down all at once. Its differentiation therefore primarily means that verses and chapters were revealed separately and gradually in accordance with the circumstances of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl). The expression tanzīl confirms this, since it denotes gradual sending down.

This temporal, gradual differentiation also entails the first sense: the Qur’an’s many teachings and rulings, initially contained in one concentrated essence and comprehensive reality, became differentiated. God rendered the Book Arabic, arranged it into verses and chapters, and revealed its portions as people’s differing capacities and readiness required, over the twenty-three years of the Prophet’s mission, so that teaching accompanied training and knowledge accompanied practice.
verses.107:
Al-Mizan explains that those given knowledge before the Qur’an include all who knew God and His communications before its revelation, whether Jews, Christians, or others. It need not be restricted to one group; but if the context confines it to followers of an un-abrogated religion, it may refer to Christian scholars who remained upon the truth without distortion.

Their prior knowledge has prepared them to understand and accept the word of truth, and has produced humility in them; the Qur’an’s recitation increases that humility. Their falling “on their faces” means prostrating on the ground. Adhqān, literally chins, are mentioned because the chin is nearest the ground in prostration, though “chin” may also stand metonymically for the whole face.
verses.108: Al-Mizan explains that they glorify God above every imperfection, especially any failure to fulfill His promise. In this context, that promise concerns the resurrection, and their affirmation opposes the polytheists’ persistent denial of resurrection and the hereafter.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains that falling on their faces and weeping manifests khuḍūʿ, the body’s outward humility and submission, while khushūʿ is the heart’s inward humility and submission. The believers described are thus humble both outwardly and inwardly. This confirms the believers’ quality mentioned in “And We reveal of the Qur’an that which is a healing and a mercy to the believers” (17:82), and contrasts with the polytheists’ denial of resurrection.

Verses 17:107-109 show that the Qur’an has no need of the polytheists’ faith. The faith of those given knowledge is evidence that it is a true Book revealed with truth, not something on which its reality or perfection depends. Belief benefits believers and rejection harms rejecters, not the Qur’an. After describing the polytheists’ aversion to the Qur’an and their demand for other signs, the commentary has shown its perfection, miraculous language and content, effect on souls, and manner of revelation; it is therefore up to them to believe or disbelieve.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that “Allah” and al-Raḥmān are names that signify the musammā but are not the reality or Essence of the musammā itself. Thus, whether one calls upon Allah or al-Raḥmān, one calls upon Him. Every one of His names is among the best names: it signifies a perfection wholly free from deficiency and evil, such as richness without need, life without death, and dominance without defeat. God possesses the pure reality of every perfection, unlike creatures who bear such qualities only with their opposites and limitations.

The pronoun in “He has the best names” refers to God’s Essence, which transcends every name and description, not to either name Allah or al-Raḥmān. The verse does not make one name encompass the rest; rather, all best names belong to God. They are means of calling upon Him and mirrors pointing to Him, so calling them is calling Him.

This establishes the Qur’anic distinction between unity of God’s Essence together with monotheism in worship, and the idolatrous combination of unity of Essence with polytheism in worship. Idolatry posits a transcendent divine essence determined into successive names through tawallud, and treats angels and jinn as the names’ influential “children” and manifestations. Since worshippers supposedly cannot reach beyond such names, they worship a name by worshipping its angelic or jinn representative; differing needs then yield differing gods. This explains the polytheists’ objection when the Prophet said, “O Allah, O Raḥmān”: they imagined that he was invoking two gods.

The verse refutes them because the names all belong to God and have no independence or separation from Him in their essence, properties, or attributes. A name serves to disclose its intended meaning, not to obstruct access to it; invoking multiple names therefore does not contradict monotheistic worship, and worship cannot terminate at a name rather than pass to the One named. Nor can God’s names, angels, or jinn be His children, for sonship entails some shared essence, quality, or perfection, while nothing can be associated with God in His Essence or perfections. Angels and jinn possess nothing independently: they are honored servants who act only by His commandment (21:26-27). All causal powers are bestowed by God, who remains their owner and has power over them.

Al-Mizan further holds that Allāh, one of the best names, originally derived from al-ilāh, an attribute meaning the worshipped being, but became a proper noun through usage and can consequently be qualified by attributes.

Regarding prayer, jahr is a very raised voice and ikhfāt a very low one; the verse first indicates a moderate course between them. It may, more apparently, instruct that prayer as a whole should not always be loud or always silent, but that some prayers should be recited aloud and others quietly, as in the Morning, Sunset, and Evening Prayers versus the remaining obligatory daily prayers. This latter reading better joins the verse’s two halves: loud recitation suggests God’s supremacy and exaltedness, quiet recitation His nearness, and their combination does justice to all His names.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains that the names which people imagine to be gods besides God are only His names and belong to Him; they possess nothing independently. Calling upon them is therefore calling upon Him, the sole Worshipped Being.

The command to praise God follows from His absolute sovereignty. Nothing resembles Him in essence or attribute: He has no son deriving from His essence or attributes, contrary to beliefs concerning angels, jinn, Christ, Ezra (ʿUzayr), or religious scholars; no partner equal to Him and sharing His kingdom; and no guardian above Him who could repair what He could not manage. There is thus no child beneath Him, partner equal to Him, or guardian above Him.

The verse praises God for this absolute sovereignty, of which the negation of sons, partners, and guardians is a consequence. It accordingly commands taḥmīd rather than merely tasbīḥ, although these negations are negative attributes that especially suit glorification. Its final, unconditional command to magnify Him, after mentioning positive and negative attributes, means that God is greater than every description. As narrated from al-Ṣādiq, Allāhu akbar means that He is greater than being described, not merely greater than everything else, since the latter would associate something else with Him in greatness. The chapter thus begins with glorification and ends with praise and magnification.
